title: Commissioners Holds Public Hearing on Licensing Kennels
author: Will Bontrager wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Commissioners holds public hearing on licensing kennels

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 773
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — The Kent County commissioners talked about not "releasing the hounds," but gave consideration to licensing their kennel, at their regularly scheduled meeting on June 24.Due to recent legislative changes, the commissioners now sit as the Fox Hunting Club Dog Kennel Licensing board.
Their first applicant was The Wicomico Hunt Club, a club in existence since the 1920s, seeking to preserve a rich history of safely hunting red foxes on horseback with hounds along fields, forest and wetlands beside rivers and tributaries of the Bay.
Approval of the application would enable the club to build the kennel for the hounds on the 20 acre Worton farm that until recently, was prohibited from housing more than five dogs since it is located in a Resource Conservation District.
Director of Planning, Housing and Zoning Bill Mackey explained that last year the club sought to change that law with an application for a text amendment.
Attorney Genevieve Macfarlane acting as counsel to the club, said the text amendment sought to create a definition for kennels specific to organized fox hunting clubs, and to amend the Zoning Ordinance to permit such kennels within the RCD zone.
However, while in that process, during a meeting with the Planning Commission, some public outcry arose concerning potential noise and safety issues over the hounds. The planning staff then recommended the commissioners hold certain licensing requirements to protect both the club and the public.
This past year, the hunt club has worked with the County to address those concerns and a text amendment was approved to allow hounds in the RCD zone on the condition a Fox Hunting Kennel Licensing Board and licensing scheme be put in place.
The county commissioners act as the oversight board and are responsible for implementing a regulatory framework specific to the licensing of such facilities.
"We've been called worse than that," Commission President Ron Fithian quipped when they were deemed the Fox Hunting Club Dog Kennel Licensing Board.
At the June 24 meeting, Deputy Director of Planning, Housing and Zoning Carla Gerber submitted the club's application for a kennel license as well as permission to build a temporary kennel to house 30 fox hunting hounds at Worton.
Gerber said the application met all the requirements as outlined in the new chapter 64 under Animals, article 62.
At these proceedings, Club Huntsman Eden Kloetzli was accompanied by supporters of the club, Attorney Genevieve Macfarlane lending counsel, Master of Fox Hounds Ed Fry, and member Dan O'Toole. Together they responded to concerns about potential noise and safety issues.
O' Toole, huntsman with Mount Carmel Hounds, stated he has been housing hounds on his Baltimore County property for 65 years. Although the area is far less rural than Kent, he has not had any issues so far. It relies on good communication with neighbors.
O' Toole has been helping design the club's kennel and suggested using mass-loaded vinyl on the fencing for effective sound proofing.
Kloetzli added that elevation changes on the property, the surrounding woods, the acoustic panelling on the fence and the natural isolation of the area, will help cut down on noise. They plan on growing a sound barrier with cedar trees as well.
Kloetzli assured them that the previous property owners of the farm had a working septic system used for cattle which would suit their purposes. Waste gets pumped out and disposed of properly and there will be no smell since they sanitize everyday.
Previously the hounds were housed at Tolchester and although challenging, Kloetzli learned from that experience, O'Toole pointed out.
Kloetzli said if the hounds are limited to what they see, they will be happy and not prone to bark as much.
Since many of these regulations are similar to the requirements they adhere to in Baltimore County, O'Toole applauded the County's process.
The club is the only recognized one on the Eastern Shore, Fry said, one of 142 clubs around the country. They adhere to Master Fox Hounds Association where they follow a strict code of how operations are run, the sanitary condition of the kennels and updated vaccinations.
The hounds all have their shots and are microchipped and soon will be wearing identifiable collars, Kloetzli pointed out.
Commission President Ron Fithian stated being a board member for dog kennel licensing is a new experience for them but by being so, if any complaints arise, they now have a system to address it.
With no voiced opposition to building the kennels during the hearing, Commissioner John Price moved to close it out. The application will be considered for a vote on July 8.
The club is cherished by many on the Eastern Shore and today, is the only remaining hunt sanctioned by the Masters of Foxhounds Association on the Delmarva Peninsula.

title: Historical Society Relationship and Regional Detention Center Update
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Historical Society relationship and Regional Detention Center update

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 389
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Denton — The Caroline County Historical Society wants to rebuild a working relationship with the County Commissioners so they can get some help funding for different projects to help bring tourist to the town."We have in and around Preston a five-mile radius the most significant components of the Underground Railroad in the United States," lifetime member of the historical society Mick McCrea said.
The Linchester Mill historical sight offers many trails and buildings to where Harriet Tubman and other prominent individuals lived.
"We have actual buildings you can literally walk in the footsteps of people where they stayed in the homes where they got freedom from," McCrea said.
Another suggestion made by historical society board member David "Gene" Harris that the Linchester Mill pond be restored for many reasons.
"If we ever had a major fire, the Linchester Mill pond would be an ideal spot to recharge their fire trucks," Harris said.
The County Commissioners want to establish a working relationship as well, a big component is funding and both sides will plan to work together in the future to help with the Linchester historical sight.
Potential Regional Detention Center updateThe potential Regional Detention Center came up in discussion again for the commissioners.
The center would be located at the former Eastern Pre-Release Unit site at 700 Flat Iron Square Road near Church Hill and would house detainees from Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties. It aims to address the growing need for modern and efficient detention facilities in the region, where counties are struggling to finance renovations or replacements of their aging detention facilities.
The commissioners said they still have not received exact numbers for how much everything will cost and how much the county will save by joining the agreement with the other counties.
Caroline County Commission Vice President Larry Porter suggested that the county should do an independent evaluation of the operating cost.
"This decision is going to depend on the operational cost and I'm talking long range operational cost," Porter said. "Would it make sense for us to engage someone to do an independent evaluation of these operating cost?"
The county also want numbers crunched on transportation, employment and other things.
"The biggest question we all have is the operating side of the detention center," Deputy Administrator Daniel Fox said.
The county will have Fox run an independent evaluation to get some calculated numbers to the administrators.

title: Liquor License Discussion Draws Large Crowd
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Liquor license discussion draws large crowd

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 779
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Rock Hall residents showed up to offer support for their local liquor store, Rock Hall Liquors & Deli, an establishment serving the area for several years with a good reputation among many. Following two hours deliberation, the Kent County Commissioners decided unanimously to grant the requested Class A liquor license for beer and wine, but not liquor — to the Rock Hall One Stop Shop — a compromise between both establishments.At the Kent County Commissioner's regularly scheduled meeting on Nov. 19, County Attorney Tom Yeager led the open session discussion of a Class A liquor license request from M&M Rock Hall, LLC, Rock Hall One Stop Shop, (formerly Shore Stop) owned by Bilal Mustafa, president and Hassan Mahmood, vice president.
Rock Hall Liquors, represented at the meeting by owner Shweta Sethi, expressed to the commissioners concerns over the gas station across the road, Rock Hall One Stop Shop, seeking a liquor license.
She was supported by a room full of Rock Hall residents along with a written petition of support from 300 town residents.
Mustafa was represented by MacLeod Law Group LLC, attorney Lance Young who stated if the application was not approved, it would set a precedent for any liquor establishment to do the same in the future.
"When somebody is dealing with government, they need to know the policies will be applied to them equally," he said of his concern that due process be ensured.
Young vouched for his clients. They are good clients, he stated, and unlike many liquor store owners, have been in the county for almost 25 years. And to meet the town's needs, they fixed the outside lights, expanded items on the menu, and agreed to stay open 24 hours, even though it would not benefit them financially.
"They are making a better establishment, which is better for Rock Hall, and so better for the county," Young said.
Representing Rock Hall Liquors, attorney from Booth, Cropper and Mariner, Lyndsey Jones Ryan, countered some of Young's points.
She claimed that between Bayside Market and Rock Hall Liquors the public need is more than met already — citing a diminishing population sinking to about 1,188, according to a 2020 census.
Ryan vouched for her client's character and dedication to their business, pointing out the family has been in the community for 19 years, working on improvements the last three years to make it nicer.
Responding to Young's claim that it would set a precedent, Ryan said these applications are considered on a "case-by-case basis," especially in a little town like Rock Hall.
And it could be a public danger as well, she claimed. If the store next door gets a liquor license, and stays open later, it could force Rock Hall Liquors & Deli to stay open longer also. With limited staff, and female employees, that could endanger them.
Adding up all these factors, Ryan was looking for Commissioners to reject the application.
Open to public comment, residents provided their input, an overwhelming majority siding with Rock Hall Liquors & Deli.
One man, living in Rock Hall for three years, appreciated the community feel of Rock Hall Liquors & Deli. He said on the contrary, he did not feel that at the other store. Under new ownership he lamented, some familiar faces were no longer there.
Many held reasons along this line. Family friendly, comfortable, they know everyone's names. The owners love the community.
Some residents noted the danger or at least public nuisance that granting a Class A Liquor license would prove. People hanging around the store at 1 a.m., stated Mark Einstein, is when alcohol becomes a problem.
Those close to the Rock Hall Liquors family, said unlike Mustafa who has other businesses in Chestertown, this is their only store, their "bread and butter," a term that was used a lot throughout the hearing.
Some giving testimony were in support of healthy competition, however they did not support a beloved Rock Hall business closing their doors, something they believed would become a reality with the granting of this license.
Yeager asked Young if his client would accept a license for beer and wine, excluding liquor. Subsequently after a brief recess, Young agreed on behalf of his One Stop Shop clients, on the condition they could return in six months to reapply for liquor to be added to the use.
Commissioner John Price acknowledged they are in full support of businesses, but supported the compromise, while warning attendees this issue will not go away in the future.
Commissioner Albert Nickerson commended the level of decorum between both parties and residents.
"In my two years, this has been the best-attended meeting," he said, "I appreciate the emotion going into this. We want to support the community, and the people that make up the community."

title: Lawsuit Compels Chestertown Council Member to Resign
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Lawsuit compels Chestertown Council member to resign

 November 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 420
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Since mid-October, the Ward 1 spot in the Chestertown Council has been vacant.The reason being that earlier this month, former council member of that ward Tim O'Brien submitted his letter of resignation after serving over three years.
O'Brien wrote, "It has been a great honor to serve on the Town Council, and I am proud of the work we have done during my term period today, November 4th, 2024, I am writing to announce that after careful deliberation regarding the best interest of the Town, I made the difficult decision to voluntarily resign from my seat on the council, effective immediately. I hope to remain active in the community, and I look forward to what's to come in the future of Chestertown."
The formal letter came on the heels of a Writ of Summons issued Oct. 18, from a Robert Miller and John and/or Jane Doe against O'Brien, according to court documents. The plaintiff's claim is that the Chestertown Charter forbids O'Brien to continue serving since he moved from Ward 1 to Ward 4, October of last year.
According to the Town Charter, Resolution 06-2023, "Councilmembers shall dwell for not less than 30 days in the ward which he is elected to represent, and in case he moves during his term of office from the ward from which he was elected, his term shall at once terminate and there shall exist a vacancy".
There was an amendment to this however, making an exception for council members moving after serving two years, but the plaintiffs claimed the amendment pertains only to new members, not those currently in office.
It would not apply to O'Brien, elected in November, 2, 2021, they state.
The plaintiffs requested not only O'Brien be removed, but all his council actions taken after the date of his move, October 23, 2023, be nullified. Attorney for the plaintiffs are Stephen Meehan, Lauren Castelli and Victoria Devore and defending O'Brien, are attorneys Lyndsey Ryan and Carly Landolfi.
O'Brien's attorneys filed for a motion to dismiss, for which a hearing will take place at the Kent County Circuit Court on Dec. 18, at 1 p.m. with Judge Harris Murphy presiding.
Chestertown Mayor David Foster and Town Administrator Larry DiRe both urged residents to help select the next Ward 1 Council member by special election on Tuesday, Jan. 21.
Residents of Ward 1 must be registered with the Kent County Board of Election Supervisors on or before Friday, Dec. 20. All Town of Chestertown residents currently registered with the County are automatically registered to vote in Town elections.

title: Chestertown Moves to Change Regulations in Historic District
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Chestertown moves to change regulations in historic district

 July 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 427
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Chestertown council member Meghan Efland, at the council's July 22 meeting with Mayor David Foster, called for a discussion with their Historic District Commission over regulations.The Historic District Commission determines, for instance, what kinds of windows can be put on a historic building. It can decide what sort of materials may be used to maintain the historical authenticity of the neighborhood.
The council unanimously decided that although they cannot veto the Historic District Commission's decisions, nor desire to, they can change the rules and regulations to on which the commission bases its decisions.
Foster was adamant he is not in anyway looking to change something that has already been decided by the Historic District Commission. But he has concerns with current regulations.
For example, he is worried about lead paint, especially on old windows.
The regulations right now allow the homeowner to put in storm windows but won't allow for brand new windows designed to look old to be placed. Foster said there's a high level of difficulty if someone wanted to put energy-efficient windows on their historic home.
Efland added roofing material has advanced as well since the regulations were written.
Efland suggested the council sit in on a Historic District Commission meeting to discuss some of the changes they'd like to see.
Right now, a Historic District Commission ruling can only be appealed at the circuit court level.
Council member Tim O'Brien said that's not the way most counties operate. Most counties, he said, have an appeal process within the town structure.
O'Brien, consulting legal over this issue, said as long as the Chestertown Planning Commission and Historic District Commission appeal to the same entity, they wouldn't have to go through the circuit court any longer.
Right now, there is a Historic District Commission ruling over the Chestertown Armory that is being appealed in the circuit court.
The council does not want to interfere with cases like that. Instead, council members agree with Efland, expressing their aim is to make these regulations more readable to the community.
"I feel like it's a lot of responsibility for that group. To have what's modern and up-to-date and to see whatever other towns are doing, I think is important," she said.
O'Brien noted that Town Manager Larry DiRe, who was absent from the meeting, has found funding to make an internal Historic District Commission appeals process possible in the near future.
For Chestertown residents interested in Historic District Commission rulings, regularly scheduled meetings are held the first Wednesday of each month at 4 p.m. in Town Hall unless otherwise announced. The meetings are also online on the town website.

title: Local legislators reflect on General Assembly
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Local legislators reflect on General Assembly

 April 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 629
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — On Wednesday morning, the Caroline County Chamber of Commerce hosted a Legislative Wrap-up Breakfast with Maryland senators and delegates from the Eastern Shore.The meeting provided a summary and discussion of the recent Maryland state legislative session, the General Assembly. Topics discussed included DAF residual legislation and solar energy.
Sens. Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline) and Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico), along with Dels. Jay Jacobs (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Steven Arentz (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), Christopher T. Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) and Jefferson Ghrist (R-36, Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), were in attendance.
Jacobs spoke on his work on the Environmental and Transportation Committee and the work both delegates and local leadership in Caroline County had on regulating dissolved air flotation, or DAF, residuals.
"I really do appreciate the fact that all three county commissioners and Caroline County were there because it had a huge impact on the committee in Annapolis," Jacobs said. "With an issue that meant that much to the county, all three county commissioners showed up and gave very compelling testimony as to the real problem."
DAF is a method for processing wastewater from food processing plants. The method leaves behind a sludge-like byproduct, or DAF residuals.
House Bill 991 and its pair, Senate Bill 1074, aim to establish a food processing residuals utilization permit authorizing the Department of Agriculture to issue the permits, develop a fee schedule and inspect any site where food processing residuals are utilized.
This bill is significant to the residents of Caroline County, who have raised concerns about the storage of dissolved air flotation residuals and other waste materials.
The Caroline County Commissioners introduced legislation on Feb. 6 to establish four moratoriums related to DAF residuals, vegetable processing wastewater and the storage of biosolids not permitted by the Department of the Environment.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter said he met with Del. Sara Love (D-Montgomery); Alan Girard, Eastern Shore director at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation; and a Caroline County Department of Planning and Codes representative to discuss the draft legislation.
The bill is awaiting final approval by Governor Wes Moore to sign into law.
SOLAR DEVELOPMENT
Delegates expressed concerns over legislation they said took away a vital part of the comprehensive solar development planning process, giving local communities less determination over solar expansion.
Jacobs spoke on Senate Bill 783, or the Brighter Tomorrow Act, which would lower the cost of developing Maryland solar projects and increase the value of solar energy for consumers across the state.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter, who was in attendance, argued that if counties are forced to have more solar, they should be able to negotiate and charge what they want from solar facilities. SB 783 attempted to limit taxes charged to commercial solar facilities.
"I made a comment in the committee: If solar was as good as we are told it's good … Why doesn't everybody in this room have it?" Arentz said. "We're pushing so hard for something we can do. And I think the General Assembly has to, at some point, wake up."
The state's Renewable Portfolio Standard had already established a nation-leading mandate to deploy solar that equals 14.5% of Maryland's electric demand by 2030. Maryland has fallen behind the pace to meet that goal, only meeting 55% of the policy's intermediate 2022 target.
After the delegates had reflected on this year's legislative session, Arentz expressed his appreciation to his fellow delegates for the work that was accomplished during the legislative session.
"I appreciate the time. You guys are wonderful. And as these guys said, this is kind of a love fest. We do it here. We do it up in Cecil County. And we're very, very lucky because we have a lot of like-minded people to communicate, we talk, and we work well together," he said.

title: Washington College Court Win Confirms Partial Demolition of Armory Will Proceed
author: Will Bontrager wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Washington College court win confirms partial demolition of armory will proceed

 September 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 591
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Chestertown Historic District Commission's May 1 decision to grant an application to Washington College to partially demolish the John H. Newnam Armory will most likely stand following a judge's ruling Wednesday.Over the summer, the college hit a speed bump in its plan to build a boutique hotel and conference center on the property that once headquartered the National Guard.
After the Historic District Commission's decision, there was a citizen's appeal made to the circuit court by residents Barbara Jorgenson, Tom Kocubinski and Steve Mitchell. They were opposed to the college's plan, favoring restoration over partial demolition.
But on Wednesday, with local Judge Harris Murphy recusing himself, visiting Judge Sidney Campen sided with the college.
Campen's decision came on the grounds that the petitioners didn't have legal standing to make their appeal.
In his opening argument, Collin Wojciechowski, an attorney representing the college, brought up a case he said was similar to this one.
Ray v. Mayor and Maryland City Council of Baltimore, he said, had "striking parallels in this matter."
In that case, citizens lived within 1,000 feet of the property, but the city still moved to dismiss the case, a move with which the Maryland Supreme Court agreed.
Unlike in that case, the petitioners, Wojciechowski claimed, can't argue by proximity since none of them live within 1,000 feet of the applicant property.
He said other than proximity, the burden of proof for the petitioners is to prove their "personal or property rights are adversely affected in a way different than the rest of the public."
"... Petitioners can't show that here. None of the history of the individuals is unique from their neighbors. That uniqueness is needed and Maryland courts have never found it to exist," Wojciechowski said.
Nelson rebutted, saying this case was indeed unique.
"There's no appellate authority that addresses the question of standing in the historic district," Nelson said.
Furthermore, he said he had actually worked the case referenced by the defense, arguing it in every stage of litigation.
That issue, he said, was a zoning decision over a 200,000-square-foot Walmart, not an historic district decision of a building constructed in 1931 in a small town.
He firmly disagreed with Wojciechowski. Residents within the Chestertown historical district are the exception, he said, because demolishing and rebuilding will affect the petitioners' taxes, property values and insurance.
Then pointing to the Historic District Commission guidelines, he read, "If an owner within the historic district allows a building to fall in disrepair, that adversely affects the character of the district."
And again in the guidelines, "The loss of any contributing historic building diminishes the district and can never be replaced."
Nelson said in this situation, the college allowed the building to go into disrepair. Additionally the Historic District Commission then violated guidelines by not issuing a written statement summarizing their decision on May 1, he said.
Combined with the written testimonies from the petitioners, it proves they should have standing, he said.
Wojciechowski countered, stating this is straightforward case, and the arguments about the Historic District Commission were merit questions, not about standing.
He said if the judge allowed this, it would set a precedent encouraging the appeal of Historic District Commission decisions.
After both sides presented their arguments, the judge agreed with Wojciechowski, dismissing the petitioner's claim.
He said Nelson did not present enough evidence or case law to show the petitioners would be adversely affected differently than any other resident in the district.
Mike Sosulski, president of the college, said he was satisfied with the judge's decision. "I think's it's the right result," he said. "While we appreciate our neighbor's position, we're pleased that the project's going forward."

title: Landowner Wants to Build Millington Camping Retreat
author: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Landowner wants to build Millington camping retreat

 November 28, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 864
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - Sandra Donnelly, owner of 32103 Millington Road, presented her plan for the 30-acre property to the Kent County Commissioners on Tuesday, Nov. 14.Accompanied by her attorney, Lance Young, with Bill Mackey the director of the Department of Planning, Housing and Zoning, they discussed Code Home Rule Bill 5-2023; a text amendment making a special exception for "outdoor retreat." Donnelly offered the commissioners an overview of her goals.She said her husband loved the property and since his death, she's looked for effective ways to use it."I'm doing this in his honor," Donnelly said.She took steps to build a camping retreat for outdoor oriented families or small groups. She aims to build 10 to 15 two-room cabins, with a central bathhouse and conduct special events yearround - maximum occupancy of two weeks.It's a simple idea, gaining popularity worldwide, requiring an amendment to a text for the commissioner's approval.Young said when Donnelly presented her idea to him, it didn't fit within the category of a country inn or a bed-and-breakfast or a retreat, so they had to introduce a new idea.Mackey explained the process that brought them before the commissioners.Donnelly's application was reviewed by the Planning Commission on Aug. 3. They gave a favorable recommendation with some added amendments.They suggested Donnelly's project consist of at least 10 acres, set back a minimum of 100 feet from the property line and recommended not to be built in the Village district.Also, the Planning and Zoning commission and Board of Appeals would review events held at the grounds on a case-by-case basis.On Sept. 6, the application worked its way to the Agricultural Advisory Commission.The agricultural commission recommended she not build on land zoned for agriculture, limiting her building to three zones: Rural Character, Rural Residential and Community Residential.Mackey explained why Donnelly's idea required a special exception in the first place."Almost all of our lodging uses are related to some sort of existing building or single structure. But this is a new idea, that there would be a variety of structures and options for people who are looking for a more outdoor experience." However, there have been issues in the region and the country with people abusing their occupancy. In many cases, getting them out has been a problematic, lengthy process.The commissioners' questions for Donnelly and Young revolved around this.Commission member Albert Nickerson asked what would prohibit the retreat from becoming a permanent village.County Attorney Tom Yeager pointed out there have been instances a seasonal campground evolved into one year-round."How would the two-week time period be enforced other than by the honor system?" he asked.Donnelly replied it's no different than someone overstaying their time in a hotel. She would call the police if that were to happen.In this case, enforcement would fall under Mackey's department as a zoning infraction.Price said enforcement, like providing an eviction notice to a tenant, is a 45-to 60-day process in most cases, and he'd prefer to prevent that.Price said, "If there's a solution or a clause we can put in to protect you and the county, I think this is an appropriate time to consider it." Donnelly agreed.Since this was a public hearing, Janet Christensen-Lewis voiced her concern over this text amendment.As the only person to sign the testimony log, she began by saying she has nothing against Donnelly but urged the commissioners to reject the text amendment.Christensen-Lewis said, "Whatever she (Donnelly) wants to do, you don't know what other people in the county are going to do, or how responsible they'll be." She echoed the commissioners sentiments, adding that enforcement policy, getting an uncooperative tenant out, is driven by complaints.If the property owner doesn't complain, or the temporary tenants don't, then how would the county know it's happening?Further, she said the county is stretched thin and does not have the resources to deal with existing zoning codes.She urged the commissioners to consider the property may soon be annexed by Millington, and hookups to water lines could pose a problem.In her closing statements, she said there are some fundamental parameters that needed consideration: the total footprint of all buildings, the determination for acreage for activities, and the definition of adequate landscaping.Donnelly addressed Christensen-Lewis' comments.She said she's willing to hook up or not hook up to certain water mains. She said that whatever taxes she needs to pay for a commercial property, she's willing.And she said that many of the things brought up in opposition to her application are worst-case scenarios.Since all events held there will be on a case-by-case basis, Donnelly doesn't see how the text amendment could be abused either.Young said Donnelly's vision fits with the county's comprehensive plan of maintaining a rural, small town character. He said the plan places an emphasis on increasing tourism and economy, supports existing businesses and aims to feature year-round attractions.All things the outdoor retreat would do, in his opinion.Fithian, although having similar questions, saw some of the potential problems brought to light were issues any business would have.The commissioners will have a third hearing during their legislative session on Dec. 19.

title: Historic Armory Could Be Torn Down to Make Way for New Boutique Hotel
author: Laura Tayman
content:
Historic Armory could be torn down to make way for new boutique hotel

 October 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 668
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Despite a new detailed presentation from Washington College President Mike Sosulski, the Chestertown Historic District Commissioners say they need still more information before approving the college's plans for the town's historic Armory building."Though we have come to the commission before, this is essentially a new request that does comply with the original deed," said Sosulski. "The Maryland Department of the Military and the Department of Public Works heartily endorse our position." The College appeared before the HDC at their Oct. 4 meeting.The Armory, built in 1931, was used for seven decades for the Maryland National Guard, as well as community events, and was put on the National Register of Historic Places in 1980. When the state declared the Armory was "surplus," the building was offered to the Town of Chestertown who did not have the resources to develop the property.Washington College bought the property in hopes of renovating the building and using it as an environmental center, right along the river. After a walk through and mold testing, the college withdrew their plans to the commission a year ago to get more information, address public input, and seek investors.Washington College president Sosulski led the new presentation last week.Sosulski said, "The college agrees that the Armory has historical significance. But it's been a constant struggle to find a purpose for this building." The college investigated several plans similar to those done with other armories throughout the state, but the costs were found to be prohibitive.Sosulski said that proposals for just stabilizing the structure cost $4 million and no investment partners could be found.At the October meeting, Sosulski provided details to this new proposal for a boutique style hotel with numerous meeting spaces that can be used by the entire community. If possible, the hotel would keep the facade of the building and keep numerous military memorabilia in prominent displays, he noted. Hersha Hospitality has agreed to partner with the company using this plan.Business leaders have been supportive of the proposal.A hotel/conference center would bring jobs, increase tourism, and help the town and county continue to improve" said Bryan Matthews, Executive Director of Kent Forward. "Our community must seize the opportunity to turn a deteriorating building with major issues into a tremendous asset." Other residents are not so sure. Resident Steven Mitchell, a facilities and environmental manager, wants the commission to have their own independent mold remediation expert to get an unbiased opinion about the mold issue. "I believe the applicant should pay for it, or the town," said Mitchell. "Or if necessary I will pay for it." Jeremy Rottweil, another resident, believed the mold remediation done before the 2005 closing took care of the mold problems, and it returned due to the college not taking proper care of the property. "Two large sump pumps and the HVAC were turned off.This is a textbook example of demolition by neglect," said Rottweil.Commission member Samantha Hollomon said she would like a current condition structural report for the head house, the main hall, and then the additions."I would like to see the cost difference between using the facade and not using it," she said."I would like to have greater clarity on the development team," said Commission member Rebecca Murphy. "If possible, to get their tax credit applications." Commissioner Monica Sella proposed the college come back before the Commission with the infrastructure costs of the project, such as building roads, getting plumbing, and so forth.Another member voiced concerns about environmental impacts from the demolition.Despite all of the questions and concerns voiced, most people in the room were supportive of the idea.Richard Keaveney, chair of the Economic Vitality Committee of Mainstreet Chestertown, told the commission that at his recent meeting, "Every member of the committee was in favor of this latest proposal." Overall, Holomon said she was "really excited" about the amount of agreement in the room. "Stay patient. Let's treat one another with respect," she advised, "This will be a group effort."

title: Caroline Commissioners Talk New Regional Detention Center
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline commissioners talk new regional detention center

 October 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 333
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — On Oct. 15 the Caroline County Commissioners discussed a plan to build a new regional detention center in Queen Anne's county.The financial burden would be split between Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties, but it is still unclear how that would be managed or what would happen to the detention center on 101 Gay Street in Denton, commissioners said at the meeting.
The new facility is being designed to hold 338 beds for men and women. The current Denton jail holds 130 inmates.
The warden of the Caroline County Detention Center, Charles Scott, said there are mental health needs among the inmates that could be better managed with a designated space, which could be incorporated into the design of the new facility.
"There should be a wing just for mental health. Juveniles and mental health are just piling up in the jail," Scott said.
He said there is plenty of land in Queen Anne's County to build this new detention center. The new facility will be located in Church Hill on the site of the Eastern Pre-Release Unit.
Commission President Travis Breeding cited the economies of scale and how the new detention center could serve the needs of the counties for less money.
The commissioners discussed who would be the authority on this tri-county project. Right now, one county commissioner and one county administrator oversee the jail in Denton. The commissioners said they wanted more clarity on how that would work in a tri-county context.
The commissioners also discussed the employment possibilities for current Caroline County Detention Center employees. Employment decisions would factor in tenure and managing workers who have fulfilled this amount of time as they work in a new county.
Scott said it is hard to find correctional officers, so everyone's job should be safe.
County Administrator Katheleen Freeman said the new facility will offer better services at lower costs, but the devil is in the details.
The commissioners agreed to discuss this further at the next meeting on Oct. 22 at the Health and Public Services building.

title: A Public Hearing Will Come for Potential Regional Detention Center
author: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com
content:
A public hearing will come for potential regional detention center

 January 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ahmad Garnett agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 449
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County wants to hear the public's opinion before making any big decisions on the potential regional detention center agreement with Kent and Queen Anne's counties.The Caroline County Commissioners discussed the draft agreement for the potential facility for the second week in a row at their weekly meeting Tuesday.
County Administrator Kathleen Freeman and County Attorney Stewart Barroll attended a meeting with Queen Anne's County officials about the draft agreement for the detention center Monday, bringing with them a list of concerns from the commissioners.
Freeman was not in attendance for Tuesday's commissioners meeting, but Barrol and Deputy County Administrator Daniel Fox presented an update on what was discussed in the meeting Monday.
Last week the commissioners' concerns largely dealt with the power Queen Anne's County would have over the regional detention center, and Queen Anne's County ability to throw Kent or Caroline County out of the agreement with no warning.
The majority of the authority over the center will be in Queen Anne's County hands, according to the draft. All decisions and disagreement must go through Queen Anne's County Commissioners, and if they may have a disagreement it will be mediated.
Under the draft, Queens Anne's County could decide after a certain amount of time to remove Caroline or Kent county from agreement, regardless of the amount of money that was put up. To remove one or both of the other counties from the agreement, according to the draft, Queen Anne's County must give the other county a two-year notice to take all their prisoners and house them somewhere else.
Those issues were discussed at the meeting on Monday, but Queen Anne's county has yet to send back the new revised draft bill.
Queen Anne's County was not receptive to all of Caroline County's requests at the Monday meeting, Barrol said, particularly a proposal to create a three-county authority to oversee the facility.
"I finally got it out of them that no, Queen Anne's will never part with any part of the title to the campus," Barrol said.
But Queen Anne's County verbally agreed to draft the agreement so that it can no longer exit the deal or force Caroline or Kent county out of the deal.
In addition, Caroline and Kent county will have the right to exit the deal if they please.
Another proposed change from Caroline County is allowing Caroline County employees positions at the regional detention center as opposed to having staff provided by just Queen Anne's County.
"From what I gather, from talking with Kathleen, that has pretty much been resolved that our employees would be able to be absorbed into the workforce," Commission Vice President Larry Porter said.
A date for a public hearing on the agreement has not yet been set.

title: Commissioner Questions Need for Iron Treatment Plant
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Commissioner questions need for iron treatment plant

 June 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 929
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Kent County Commission President Ron Fithian said they are still uncommitted to building a $4.5 million facility to remove iron from the groundwater near the Nicholson landfill in Chestertown.Fithian said before any kind of construction begins, someone from the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) has to come here and give the county a suitable explanation why they need this plant.
Since the landfill was closed and capped about a decade ago, the county has been responsible for testing near the site for the presence of any contaminants leaching into the groundwater.
Director of Public Works Dan Mattson said VOCs or volatile organic compounds were identified about 10 years ago. Recent testing shows the current treatment plan is functioning as designed, regulating pH and reducing copper.
The project scope at that time did not include standards for iron, he said. With new standards in place by MDE, current testing does not place water samples within the range of compliance.
"The project would create a net benefit for iron levels reaching the stream, in that it brings us to compliance," Mattson said.
Originally projected to cost $2.7 million, the price tag of such a system to mitigate iron levels has nearly doubled, Mattson explained.
In order to help pay for this facility, former public works director and now consultant, Mike Moulds and Mattson are working with the USDA to obtain an increased funding obligation in the amount of approximately $1.7 million. They've been hustling, Moulds said, and they faced a deadline of June 19, to secure some funds.
Mattson and Moulds requested the commissioners sign a letter of intent to meet the conditions of the financing as well as the USDA request for obligation of funds forms.
Signing it would keep public works from repeating the bidding, potentially costing the county more money, Moulds put.
Although Fithian sympathized with the position of the public works personnel, he was hesitant to sign anything, especially when he can't see how that facility would fix iron in the water.
He stated there are geological reasons.
Kent County is drawn on aquifers, or porous rock or sediment saturated with groundwater, that are inundated with iron, Fithian said.
Not just at Nicholson Landfill.
Fithian said the groundwater "everywhere" contains iron because it's in the stone surrounding the water; that stone creates iron.
If iron is in the groundwater throughout the county, what good is stopping it at one specific area, Fithian queried. "Every well in the whole county is inundated with iron. I am baffled as to what this project would do," Fithian said.
Talking to residents, many feel the same, he said. Iron in the water's common in the county, he said, "We all deal with it."
We put salt in the conditioner, a more cost-efficient solution than the $4.5 and the continual costs of operations, he stated.
Despite his opinion, Fithian said he's willing to listen to MDE.
Moulds, not disagreeing, explained it from their side. Not only is there a deadline that if not reached, could compromise the bid, but there are penalty fees as well.
Monthly penalty costs MDE puts on them for having iron in the water.
Moulds pointed out those fees will continue if iron's in the water.
And there's no guarantee fees won't go up in the future.
At the crux of the issue, Fithian isn't convinced such a facility would solve the iron issue — since the outlined plans have the treated water pumping into an adjacent ditch which would result in the treated water flowing back into the ground then going through the aquifer thereby adding iron back into the water.
The commissioners asked if signing the letter of intent could pressure them into building the facility. County Attorney Tom Yeager said traditionally, signing a letter of intent showed good faith to all parties concerned, but language could possibly be changed in the contract to make it conditional.
In Fithian's opinion, the best way to speed along the process is "to get someone from MDE here."
"I think we're supposed to operate like that. I would think that the county citizens would hope that we have clarification when we spend $4.5 million dollars. And it may be perfectly legitimate, but I'm going to have to hear it."
Commission members Albert Nickerson and John Price backed the president.
Price said, "It only makes good common sense. Why all the sudden after 30 years is this a big deal?"
"It's our responsibility to talk to our constituents why we're spending this," Nickerson added, "Because the 'state said so,' is not good enough in this instance."
County Administrator Shelley Heller said they reached out to the MDE Secretary Serena McIlwain who offered to talk to Fithian privately. Fithian refused that, saying the public should be in on the conversation.
Ultimately, the commission agreed to sign the letter of intent in order to not impede the process Moulds and Mattson had undergone already. However, their agreement was conditional on MDE explaining the project in a satisfactory manner.
Price made the motion to "approve the execution of the USDA letter of intent to meet the conditions and request for obligations of funds forms for the Nicholson Landfill remediation project contingent upon satisfactory answers from MDE regarding the project and why it needs to be done and approval of a contractor if we decide to move forward."
Meeting with unanimous approval, the commissioners were clear, this in no way means they agreed to build the treatment facility.
Fithian said when Governor Wes Moore visited last, he said to reach out if there's ever an issue. Until now the commission president hasn't, but if the MDE secretary doesn't attend in person or send a representative, it could be time to make that call.

title: On the River - Heritage Trail on Chester River Aims to Improve Access, Promote History, Fishing, Boating
author: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
On the river - Heritage Trail on Chester River aims to improve access, promote history, fishing, boating

 October 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com | Page: 28 | Section: News

 CHESTERTOWN - The Chestertown Heritage Trail is a project aimed at improving public access to the picturesque wetlands along the Chester River. It's rooted in the Chestertown Comprehensive Plan which, among other things, emphasizes the need to have more publicly-acces-sible land.Throughout history the river played a pivotal role for Native American communities, European settlers, and for both free and enslaved Africans - while also a critical asset to the region's agricultural economy.In the proposal letter sent by the Chestertown Council to the Kent County Commissioners, that sentiment is echoed. "Today the Chester River remains an integral part of the community, supporting recreational, educational, and economic activities like boating, fishing and crabbing," it stated.As of Oct. 11, the Council requested from the County, $350,000 to initiate Phase 1 of the Chestertown Heritage Trail plan. If approved, sections will be designed to cross wetland areas near the Washington College pavilion and the area south of the Armory site at 509 S Cross Street, Chestertown.The first phase involves detailed engineering, design and construction of the initial trail section. The 1,000 foot-long section consists of a bike and walking trail along with an observation platform for optimal river viewing.With the goal of creating an "environ-mentally-conscious and aesthetically pleasing trail," the project team will ensure all safety and accessibility measures are met.The initial drawings and designs can then be carried into future designs. Phase 2 seeks to expand public access along the wetlands, with a focus on recreational and educational opportunities.For example, the trail will be co-located with the site ofWashington College's Semans-Griswold Environmental Hall, which is a regional hub for research.Washington College's Chief of Staff and Vice President for Planning and Policy, Victor Sensenig said the trail also fits into their plans as well."We see it as fulfilling the long-term goals for the college's waterfront, and the public accessibility component of the project supports one of the goals of our new strategic plan, which calls for strengthened relationships with the town, county, and region."He added over the last decade, the college has made significant investment in a beautiful waterfront campus, and expressed enthusiasm about the prospect of welcoming more of the community to enjoy that space.In that space, during Phase 2, more trails can be added, beyond the Armory, to Radcliffe Creek. Ultimately, plans are to connect the Heritage Trail with the Rail to Trail network, known also as the Gilchrest Rail Trail.The council's proposal also notes opportunities for public art installations, scenic viewpoints, and educational elements integrated throughout.H erz said earlier in the year, the commissioners supported the project. He's hoping they'll do so again.In the request to the County, Herz included a letter dated March 2, to U.S. Sen. Ben Cardin, detailing the Kent County Commissioners' support of the trail project -$750,000 was requested at that time. In that letter, the County appreciated the importance of public waterfront access as well as any economic development it could bring.That original request was denied by Cardin, said Herz, but they were encouraged to re-apply.Now for a lesser amount, the Council is hopeful of the proposal being included in the 2024 state legislative agenda.Some potential funding sources include: Community Parks and Playground grants, Federal Land and Water Conservation Fund, Program Open Space, and the Rural Legacy Program.The next milestone date, Herz said, is Oct. 24 on which day Council will offer an in-person presentation of these materials to the county commissioners.H erz sees the importance of the project, "The Chestertown Heritage Trail represents a significant step toward enhancing local access to the Chester River, creating opportunities for connection to nature, appreciation of our heritage, and enjoyment of the scenic beauty the Chester offers."

title: Counties Approve Chesapeake College Budget Request, Shift Cost of Tech Center
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Counties approve Chesapeake College budget request, shift cost of tech center

 April 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 526
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — In a joint meeting Thursday, officials across Caroline, Dorchester, Kent, Queen Anne's and Talbot counties approved a shift in county cost shares for Chesapeake College's new technical building.During the meeting, which was held at the college's main campus in Queen Anne's County, the five counties approved a total $9.02 million budget request made by the college for fiscal year 2026. The school's budget is $1.31 million higher than its fiscal year 2025 budget.
Part of the $9.02 million budget request included a $952,560 request for the design of a new technical building. Chesapeake College Vice President for Administrative Services Karen Smith said the new building will have areas for a variety of programs, including agriculture, electrical, welding and fabrication, construction trades and advanced manufacturing. She said the cost for the design phase could be lower depending on state approval.
Although the five counties approved the request for funding for the design, the decision came with a shift in contributions toward the project.
Dorchester County's share of costs for the design phase will be taken on by Queen Anne's County. This means Queen Anne's County's responsibility for the project will jump from 28.9%, or an estimated $275,290, to 47.8%, or an estimated $455,324.
During the meeting, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer and Vice President Mike Detmer outlined their council's concerns regarding paying for the project.
Although other counties hope to use the new technical building for career and technical education at the high school level, Dorchester County has a career and technology center it is still paying off, they said.
Through its budget process, Dorchester County has struggled to eliminate an estimated $6.2 million deficit.
Pfeffer said Dorchester County takes in about $45 million in property and income taxes and will have to give Dorchester County Public Schools $26.6 million for fiscal year 2026.
"So we're trying to run the rest of the county on half of that," he said. "So while in conceptual context, we believe in the project, fiscally our citizens and our staff are saying we don't know how we're going to be able to participate."
At the Chesapeake College meeting, Queen Anne's County Commissioner Jack Wilson Jr. shared his county's decision to cover Dorchester County for the project design costs.
"We all know what happens if we let this money go back to the state," Wilson said. "It's going to go somewhere else in this state, and it's not going to be here. We got this far. And Lenny, listen, I feel for you guys. I know what you're going through. But I think we just need to keep it on the rails at least through the design phase and see what the state's going to help with."
According to documents from the meeting, the state will support 75% of project costs, and the counties will support the remaining 25%.
After the counties voted to approve the amended capital budget, Kent County Commission President Ron Fithian said he understands the position Dorchester County is in, mentioning the Blueprint for Maryland's Future and "unfunded mandates" by the state.
"I think we all understand any one of us could be in your same position very easily," Fithian told the Dorchester County Council members.

title: How ARPA Funds Shaped Maryland's Mid-Shore

How ARPA funds shaped Maryland’s Mid-Shore

 Read News Document

 Delegate Jay Jacobs, who represents Maryland's District 36 — encompassing Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil and Caroline counties — has seen the region through economic peaks and valleys. But the COVID-19 pandemic presented a crisis unlike any other.At the same time, it brought a rare opportunity.
Through the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), Maryland received $3.7 billion in federal relief funds. Jacobs estimated that roughly $88 million of that flowed into his district over the past five years.
"The money gave counties and municipalities a chance to get things done when they normally might not have had that opportunity," Jacobs said.
Across the district, more than 200 projects were funded through ARPA, aimed at bolstering local infrastructure, supporting nonprofits and modernizing essential services.
Rock Hall to Queen Anne's: Local Needs, Local SolutionsEach town took a unique approach, reflecting ARPA's flexible framework.
In Rock Hall, the town's aging wastewater system was a priority. Mayor James Cook said of the $1.3 million received, $300,000 went toward replacing the headworks at the sewer plant — a key filter that removes debris such as grease and rags from wastewater.
Chestertown formed a task force led by Ward 2 Council member Tom Herz to ensure transparency and community input. Of the $4.25 million allocated, local nonprofits were invited to align funding requests with the town's comprehensive plan.
In Galena, $570,000 supported road improvements designed to make parks more accessible and attract visitors.
Betterton directed its $311,000 toward modernizing its website to be ADA-compliant, enabling online payments, purchasing an air purifying unit, and upgrading pump stations with generators for resilience.
Millington received $504,821, though specific projects were not detailed.
Queen Anne's County saw one of the largest allocations: $16.3 million. Projects included installing 3,300 feet of water line at the Old Towne Shopping Center, investing $900,000 to upgrade affordable housing units, and expanding broadband access with $1.5 million. Six new consoles were also added to the county's 911 backup center, and cell phone boosters were installed in public schools to strengthen communication in rural areas.
Countywide Efforts and Broadband ExpansionIn Cecil County, where municipalities received a greater share of ARPA funds than the county itself, a major initiative focused on expanding high-speed internet. A $16.2 million broadband project combined $12.8 million in state funds, $2.5 million from internet service providers, and $900,000 in ARPA funds contributed by the county.
According to county officials, additional ARPA investments went toward two emergency medical services paramedic stations and a new training center for the Cecil County Sheriff's Office.
Rising Sun used $2,300 for infrastructure repairs, while the Town of North East applied its share to enhance police department operations.
In Caroline County, which received just under $6.5 million, part of the funding was used for infrastructure, while a portion supported reentry programs and post-release case management for individuals leaving the Ordnance Road Detention Facility.
Jacobs noted that ARPA's flexibility was one of its most valuable aspects.
"It was not one size fits all," he said. "Municipalities could use the money to meet their specific needs — with the only caveat being it must be spent by Dec. 31, 2026."
As ARPA Winds Down, Financial Pressure MountsNow, with the funding window closing, local governments are bracing for its absence. Jacobs said the drying up of ARPA funds is intensifying pressure on the state as the General Assembly works to pass the FY 2026 budget — which currently faces a $3.5 billion shortfall.
"Certain services were being relied on and now are cut off," Jacobs said. "ARPA funds possibly would have kept some of these programs afloat."
A notable cut is the reduction in senior care funding by the Maryland Department of Aging. Jacobs said the proposed $2.5 million budget — an 18% reduction — could translate to about $28,000 less per county. He warned this could destabilize staffing and services for vulnerable seniors, such as in-home care, transportation and meal delivery.
"These cuts will be felt, not by the lawmakers, but by ordinary hardworking folks who have to make decisions about affording food or putting gas in the car," he said.
Talbot County: Planning for LongevityTalbot County took a strategic approach. Officials distributed surveys to identify community priorities, which included broadband access, public health, and household assistance.
According to Cassandra Vanhooser, director of Talbot County Economic Development and Tourism, the county received about $7.2 million in ARPA funds. The goal, she said, was to ensure that projects wouldn't falter once federal dollars were gone.
"These are largely capital items, these are one-time items... a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity," said then Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher. "We need to be very careful about how this is done."
Among Talbot's allocations:
- $1.75 million to Easton Utilities' Connect Talbot project to expand broadband to rural residents.
- $105,000 to the Chesapeake Center in Easton to replace a failing septic system and connect to county sewer.
- $500,000 in grants for volunteer fire company equipment upgrades.
"People recognize that this is transformational money," Vanhooser said at the time of the funding discussion, "It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to be a driving force for change and to impact the lives of our citizens."
Looking AheadAs the Dec. 31, 2024 obligation deadline nears, and the Dec. 31, 2026 expenditure deadline looms, local leaders are focused on maximizing remaining funds while grappling with what comes next.
Jacobs is urging urgency from lawmakers.
"With less than 20 days in session," he said, "the Assembly needs to come up with solutions — and fast."

title: Proposed Tax Breaks Could Mean Service Cuts in Lower-Income Counties
author: Paul Kiefer Capital News Service
content:
Proposed tax breaks could mean service cuts in lower-income counties

 March 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: PAUL KIEFER Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 963
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Gov. Wes Moore plans to change how Marylanders take deductions on their state income taxes, but officials in some of the state's poorest counties say that plan could force them to cut services."You mentioned that the federal government is creating chaos for our state government in an effort to balance their budget," Del. Jefferson Ghrist, a Republican representing Caroline, Cecil, Kent and Queen Anne's Counties, told Gov. Moore in a recent budget hearing. "It appears that your budget does sort of the same thing to our county governments."
Moore's administration, however, contends that the reforms will provide tax relief to a majority of Marylanders — including residents of lower-income counties — even if those county governments face a revenue loss.
"This proposal leaves more cash in the pockets of the majority of Maryland's households," said Budget and Management Secretary Helene Grady.
Lawmakers in Annapolis are weighing a two-pronged approach to tax reform intended to shift the scales in favor of low- and middle-income households.
Moore's proposal to double the state's standard deduction would provide a tax break to Marylanders who opt not to itemize their income tax deductions — many of them low- and middle-income. To account for the resulting revenue loss, the governor's office proposes ending the practice of itemized deductions, which would mean a larger income tax bill for many high-income Marylanders.
But county governments also collect income taxes, and a tax break for lower-income Marylanders would deal a blow to some counties' budgets.
Representatives from Allegany County appeared in Annapolis last week to ask lawmakers to soften that blow.
"Governor Moore discussed the idea that no Marylanders should be left behind," Allegany County Attorney T. Lee Beeman told lawmakers on Friday. "Ultimately, his proposal this year will do exactly that in Allegany County. It will leave Allegany County behind."
If the General Assembly moves forward with doubling the standard deduction, Allegany County would stand to lose $3.2 million in revenue next year, according to Maryland's Board of Revenue Estimates.
While the vast majority of county residents would receive a tax cut, "we'll be looking at probably cutting potentially each and every service we have," said Allegany County Administrator Jason Bennett. "We're pretty slim as it is."
Last year, the county laid off emergency services staff and scaled back employee health insurance in response to a $13 million deficit. Additional cuts could mean scaling back snow clearance operations in the winter, public transit service and support for the county's library service, he told Capital News Service.
If Allegany County raised local income taxes to the maximum rate allowed under Maryland law, he added, the county could only make up for half of the projected losses created by doubling the standard deduction.
Allegany County is not alone. Del. Malcolm Ruff, a Democrat representing Baltimore City, noted that doubling the standard deduction could undercut services in his district.
"Baltimore City would lose approximately $40 million over the next five years based on those changes," Ruff said.
The Board of Revenue Estimates projects that half of Maryland's counties and county equivalents would lose income tax revenue if the state moves forward with the proposed changes to deductions. Those include all but one of the 10 poorest Maryland counties as of the Census Bureau's 2023 American Community Survey.
"Contrast that with our friends in the beltway corridor," said Beeman. "Montgomery County stands to gain $300 million in income tax revenue over the next five years. It's a shocking contrast."
Meanwhile, some members of the Legislative Black Caucus of Maryland have expressed concerns that eliminating itemized deductions would have a disproportionate impact on majority-Black districts in the Washington suburbs.
Residents of Charles and Prince George's Counties itemize their deductions at higher rates than residents of any other Maryland counties. That presents a political challenge for someone like Sen. Michael Jackson, a Democrat representing parts of Calvert, Charles and Prince George's Counties. Residents in those districts are more likely than other Marylanders to see their tax bills increase under Moore's plan.
Jackson told CNS that he and other caucus members representing those counties are in talks with the governor to address their concerns.
But Moore's current proposals drew praise from some outside observers.
"Itemized deductions are regressive," said Miles Trinidad, a state policy analyst with the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan think tank. "These policies offer the largest benefits to higher income taxpayers and little if any benefits to low- and middle-income families."
Grady, meanwhile, notes that the governor's tax reforms would offer a tax cut to a majority of Marylanders, and that aid to local governments accounts for a third of general fund expenses in the proposed 2026 budget — aid that would support both public school systems and county governments.
The governor's office also underscores that Maryland's standard deduction is only a third of Virginia's, meaning that some poor and working-class residents who would pay no income tax in Virginia make enough to pay income tax in Maryland.
While Moore's proposal would still leave Maryland's standard deduction lower than those in Virginia and Washington, his office argues the change is in the interest of fairness.
However, given the dire state of Maryland's budget and the prospect of dwindling federal support, Grady also noted that the state may not be in a position to simultaneously offer tax cuts to most Marylanders and shield counties from the statewide budget crunch.
"Given the general fund challenge, it would be very difficult to insulate counties entirely from impacts," she said.
Senate President Bill Ferguson, a Democrat representing Baltimore City, echoed Grady's sentiment.
"I appreciate [the governor's] approach of bringing forth a proposal that attempted to balance state needs, local needs and our business climate," he said. "But we're dealing with an unprecedented situation, and so just as the state is having to tighten the belt. I think local jurisdictions are going to be in a similar place this upcoming year."

title: MACo Officials Say Cost Shifts from State to Counties Are 'Absurd,' Unfair
author: Konner Metz
content:
MACo officials say cost shifts from state to counties are 'absurd,' unfair

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 647
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Representatives from the Maryland Association of Counties minced no words when speaking to the Eastern Shore's state legislators Friday morning about the expected cost burdens being placed on counties this budget cycle."Shifting these costs onto counties at this point is absurd," said Kevin Kinnally, the association's legislative director.
Earlier this month, the Department of Legislative Services told the Eastern Shore Delegation that local governments across the state may have to pick up around $144 million in costs as the state legislature and Gov. Wes Moore grapple with tackling a near $3 billion deficit.
The governor's proposed fiscal year 2026 budget would shift costs in a number of areas, including teacher pensions and property assessments, according to MACo officials.
In Caroline and Talbot counties, projected local cost shifts are in the $700,000 range, per legislative services projections. Dorchester County is at $830,000, while Queen Anne's County leads the pack for the Mid-Shore at $970,000. Kent is the lowest of the five counties with a $300,000 projection.
Friday at the Eastern Shore Delegation meeting, Kinnally said the Shore's poorer counties, like Caroline and Dorchester, are being "railroaded."
Kinnally claims the state budget leaves counties with no choice but to raise property tax rates, going so far as to deem it a "state-mandated property tax increase."
"Two-thirds of Marylanders live in counties at the maximum local income tax rate, so the only place to go is to the property tax," Kinnally said. "Which is regressive, which everybody hates. But they're pushing us into a corner here, and that's not fair."
Michael Sanderson, executive director of MACo, said the organization took a closer look at how cost shifts would impact Dorchester County's fiscal situation.
After running the numbers, Sanderson said he believes Dorchester County may have to raise property taxes, a result he called "absolutely bonkers."
"I have no idea how Dorchester County manages this year's budget," Sanderson said.
SOLAR COMPROMISEAs legislators and industry leaders have eyes on a joint hearing Friday regarding the state's solar legislation, MACo is opposing Senate Bill 931 and its paired House bill.
The legislation is designed to expand solar energy across the state, a measure intended to work toward accomplishing Moore's clean energy goals for Maryland. If passed, the bill would give the state authority to approve solar energy projects — a significant harm to local siting authority, critics say.
Dominic Butchko, MACo's intergovernmental relations director, said the association opposes the legislation based on five impacted areas: safety, livability of rural areas, concerns for local taxpayers, affordable housing opportunities being stripped and inefficiencies in the legislation's requirements.
Butchko said the legislation strays from compromises MACo thought it reached last November.
But through recent discussions with solar industry leaders and environmental advocates, Butchko still sees a path to compromise.
"Those efforts have started to yield some fruit," Butchko said. "We believe we actually have amendments that revert the legislation back to where we were at or pretty close to where we were at in November."
MUNICIPAL LEAGUE
Friday, the Eastern Shore Delegation heard a brief update from the Maryland Municipal League, an organization representing local municipal governments.
The group has two legislative priorities this session: Senate Bill 390, which would allow local governments to have trained civilians issue speed camera citations instead of police officers; and House Bill 991, which would allow local governments to institute food and beverage fees.
Justin Fiore, the league's deputy director of advocacy and public affairs, said House Bill 991 could give flexibility to governments that are "heavily dependent on property taxes as (their) only revenue."
"We have 43 million visitors annually to the state of Maryland, and while they do pay a hotel tax if they stay, we really don't capture revenue from the services that they utilize," Fiore said.
The food and beverage fee bill is still waiting committee review and House approval before it moves to the Senate, while the speed camera citation bill was passed by the Senate earlier this month and currently sits in the House.

title: Galena Passes Budget While Starting First Time Investment
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Galena passes budget while starting first time investment

 June 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News

 GALENA — After a public hearing for the budget where no members of the public attended, Mayor John Carroll and the Galena Town Council on Monday night passed the ordinance to their fiscal year 2025 budget.The total allocations divided between fund categories: General, $553,250; Sewer, $342,246; and Water, $173,675 — for a combined total of $1,069,171 matched their total income for a balanced budget.
The town budget includes a tax revenue of $258,000, alongside $76,678 in receivables for utilities.
The property tax rate, Carroll said, remains set at .0222 per $100 of assessed value. There was no increase in taxes, no increase for additional fees, water or in trash and recycling.
Town Attorney Tom Yeager reminded the council they were passing the ordinance to pass the budget.
Ultimately, they approved of ordinance 2024-01FY-25 Budget.
Also during this budget session, the town embarked for the first time in investing. They decided to take some money out of their savings and place it in an interest bearing certificate of deposit account.
Financial and Administrative Clerk Marisa Pisapia, while bringing up various line items, got the attention of the council about this. Once they scoured places to invest they chose to secure their investment with PNC Bank for eight months at a 4.65% interest rate.
Council member Sarah Merrell made it official.
"I make a motion to authorize doing a CD out of our water savings account," she said.
The motion passed unanimously.
Carroll detailed the next step in the process. Right before they leave for the Maryland Municipal League June 23 — 26 in Ocean City, they'll meet with someone from PNC Bank. From there they'll set up an account to get things in motion.
As a first, reiterated Carroll, "we're dipping our toes in it."
In other financial matters, Grants Coordinator and Tech Support Grant Audrey Erschen talked about the various grants she's been working on.
She received notification their Teen Play Area was included in the State of Maryland's FY2025 Budget, and must be approved by the Maryland Board of Public Works. The grant was for climbing equipment and installation.
They were not awarded this year on their No Gym, Think Outside Application, but she'll try again next year.
And in the tech department, she was informed they would not have to replace their Quick Books until 2026 — a relief for the council.
Maintenance and Facilities Coordinator Warren Walters had updates of his own particularly concerning the wastewater treatment plant. They had removed 42.55 tons of sludge in 2024, with a total cost of $2,957.24. Total effluent gallons (liquid waste or sewage discharged) discharged were 3,873,000 and daily average effluent gallons were 25,463.
Carroll who wanted to get a general idea, said, "It looks like we're averaging 25,000 gallons or so. That's what I wanted to see, where we're truly at. I want to know what our capacity is always. And when it fluctuates during a certain point of time."
Walters, working with Erschen, said his goal going ahead is in mitigation procedures, aiming to reduce the production of methane and leachate that can contaminate surface waters. This process involves managing wastewater at its source, which can include water conservation and recycling.
Walters is in conversations with the Environmental Protection Agency, so the town possibly won't have to spend money on the mitigation process. Carroll thought that a good idea, and mentioned that he's been talking with the University of Maryland Finance Center too. The idea is once they have their survey complete, they'll open up the conversation even more.
"We can attack it from both angles," Carroll said, "state and federal."
After hearing updates on all departments, Yeager commended the council on their work.
Carroll noted the completion of the budget was a team effort.
The Galena Town Council's next meeting will be on Monday, July 1. See more information at townofgalena.com.
