title: Salary, Retention Hot Topics Before Commissioners
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Salary, retention hot topics before commissioners

 September 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 875
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - The high turnover rate in county government jobs is an ongoing issue, according to Kent County Commission President Ron Fithian.Director of Human Resources, Jim Miller, confirmed that when they met on Aug. 29."In the past five or six months we've lost eight people," he said, adding all of them were in the public works department.Six left, he said, entirely based on money."It's been 25 years we've had this problem. If we don't do something to correct it, we're going to have this problem for another 25 years," Fithian reminded those in attendance.The president of the commission had previously asked Miller to look into switching from a percentage salary, the system currently in place, to a flat rate salary for their employees.Miller had ample time to research the subject, Fithian said."What we're finding with the ad-hoc survey we conducted is, the salaries for the lower positions are significantly behind on the competition.So if we give them a flat rate, it wouldn't make a difference." Miller determined this by comparing a year's salary based on percentage increases with that of a flat rate hypothetically begun on that same date."I took a look at the increases those employees who left got, using the percentage for July 1, and compared that to if we had given them the flat rate that had been done a year prior." His findings: the difference on average was just $140 a year.Miller pointed out, because the market offered employees a 7-12, percentage increase to go elsewhere, a flat rate would not "stave off the turnover," they've experienced.Fithian pushed back a little, exclaiming it depends on what the flat rate is."To say it wouldn't make a difference, I don't think that's exactly right. It depends on what you give them." And Fithian said they have some control over that."We generally have a certain amount of money for salaries. If we're losing people at the $35,000 or $40,000 mark, you would obviously make the flat rate higher for them and less for people at the higher end of the scale." He emphasized these kinds of jobs are highly important. Losing them would be problematic."You think that people working for the county roads aren't worth the cost, do without them for a year and see what happens." Miller agreed with Fithian, saying the amount of the flat tax rate makes a difference. However, Miller predicted they'll find the price of certain jobs have been out-priced. He said that the scale and the ranges are off; the scale hasn't kept up with the market.For example, he said a job like Motor Equipment Operator, MEO, class 1, that the market says should be $40,000 a year might be classed in the county as $35,000 a year."We have to take a look at the entire structure. We can't just grab one position out of a grade that has six or seven jobs in it, because what do you do about the other five or six jobs," Miller said.Commissioner John Price and County Attorney Tom Yeager, said they would prefer seeing a form of salary based on job performance, like a step-system.Miller, having experience with that, said the problem with a step-system is it's "entirely unrelated to performance." He suggested if they want something based on performance, it would be better to have a career ladder instead. That, however, he added, only benefits the larger departments, such as the Department of Public Works, not Human Resources, like Miller's team.It's not the mode of the salary that is the major problem, Miller noted.Whether it's a flat rate, a step system or a career ladder, it's more about matching the competitor's prices.In that ad-hoc study, he pointed out the promise of better benefits does not attract and retain people either."It's great to have them, and in 30 years to have a pension plan, but not for someone taking their first job out of school." Their questions are immediate, Miller added.A person just out of college, he said, is more concerned about how to pay the rent. Or buy their first house.Or have enough to buy groceries and get gas in this economy."Today's issues," Miller stated.He said despite the County's benefits being second to-none, they aren't addressing the salary piece of it.What will, is an extensive study."We're about to engage in a salary study through the Maryland counties, where we'll be able to not just talk about salary increases as a function as an annual review, but discuss where we need to be in the market place to be competitive to attract and retain." The study, he pointed out, will be finished in time for the FY25 budget discussion.Based on all of Miller's research, a flat rate, as it is priced right now, is not the answer."It's not keeping up with where the market has gone for us," Miller stated.His recommendation to the commissioners was to continue percentage increases as opposed to flat rate amounts, for right now.Fithian added, "We'd love for everybody working out of here to be happy with their salaries. Unfortunately that's not the case, but it definitely needs to be looked at." That's something Miller confirmed he'd do, saying it's on the top list of his priorities.

 ANNAPOLIS — The three Republican delegates representing Maryland's District 36 — Steve Arentz of Queen Anne's County, Jay Jacobs of Kent County and Jeff Ghrist of Caroline County — formally filed for reelection Wednesday."The District 36 team, which also includes Senate Minority Leader Steve Hershey, has long worked together to advance fiscal responsibility, economic growth, local infrastructure investment and policies that protect the values and livelihoods of the Shore's families and businesses," the incumbents said in a joint press release Wednesday. "Their record reflects years of collaboration and dedication to Caroline, Cecil, Kent and Queen Anne's counties."
Arentz, who has served as a District 36 representative since 2013, when he was appointed to fill the seat vacated by now Sen. Steve Hershey, underscored his focus on economic development and local business growth in the press release.

I am running for reelection because there is more work to do to strengthen our economy and preserve our way of life."
Jacobs was mayor of Rock Hall before being sworn in as a District 36 representative in 2010. In the press release, he emphasized his "commitment to protecting the Shore's values."
"Representing the people of District 36 is the honor of a lifetime," Jacobs said. "Our constituents expect us to fight for common sense, to push back against Annapolis overreach, and to ensure that rural Maryland is never forgotten.  CENTREVILLE — Wrapping up National Rebuilding Month and celebrating its first appreciation lunch following its merger, Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore recognized volunteers and supporters at the Centreville United Methodist Church April 26.Rebuilding Together Eastern Shore provides free, critical home repairs for income eligible homeowners in Kent and Queen Anne's counties the whole month of April kicked projects into high gear to provide vital repair needs across the area, completing six projects including fresh off of two that very Saturday, said co-President Larisa Thomas.
Providing more resources and personnel to help more residents, the recent merge of the Kent and Queen Anne's counties departments has made Rebuilding Together even stronger together, Thomas said.
Thomas started as a volunteer swinging a hammer 15 years ago and credited the non-profit as making a difference in local lives.
Before rebranding, Rebuilding Together originated nationally as Christmas in April in 1973 and started in Queen Anne's County in 1994 and in Kent Count in 2004, according to Executive Director Genevieve Croker in a presentation to the Queen Anne's County Commissioners April 22.
Keeping the human aspect along with the housing aspect, Rebuilding Together recognizes everyone has the right to live comfortably, and works to repair homes, revitalize communities, and rebuild lives, Croker said.
All work is done at no cost to the homeowners who meet the income limits and other criteria. Typical projects can include painting, installing ramps and grab bars, repairing floors, plumbing, electrical, and other areas needed to ensure safe and healthy housing for homeowners.
"We say what we're going to do," Community Service Coordinator Cory Palmer said.
Rebuilding Together seeks to establish safe homes and communities for all and addresses the housing crisis by improving property values and preserving affordable housing stock, noting it is often cheaper to repair a home than build a new one and help aging homeowners age in place, Croker said.
Helen Fisher, of Crumpton, was one such homeowner utilizing volunteer services including smoke detector installation, outside lighting installation, and improved home skirting. At the appreciation luncheon, Fisher credited volunteers as professionals who get the job done.
Rebuilding Together welcomes volunteers of all calibers, whether with repairs or behind the scenes fundraising. "There is a role available for you," Thomas said.
Palmer encouraged anyone struggling with home repair costs to apply for services, noting income requirements and guidelines can change.
Volunteer Dan Hercher, of Church Hill, recently celebrated his first completed project with Rebuilding Together. Experienced with repair work, he said he loved seeing the change made to the homes and what it means to the homeowners.
"Some people don't have the tools or resources, so it's nice to help," he said.

Groundbreaking of Millington Senior Village attended by Secretary Day

 MILLINGTON — "I am proud of what we achieved and am looking forward to this project coming to life and bearing fruit," Millington Mayor Kevin Hemstock told an audience of stakeholders and community leaders on Dec. 3, about the new senior housing center being built. The new facility will be located at 172 Sassafras Street — the site of the former Millington Elementary School.He along with Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) Secretary Jake Day, Chair of Home Partnership Inc. Phil Wohlfort and Kent County Commissioners Ron Fithian, John Price and Albert Nickerson, tossed out the first shovelfuls of dirt.
"As we break ground today, it's not just the beginning of a building project, I think this is going to be important for a lot of people in Millington," Hemstock said.
Earlier, inside the building of the school, in a spacious room with walls that still had paintings of emblematic characters from childhood, Clifford the Big Red Dog, The Wizard of Oz, Winnie the Pooh and Bambi, Hemstock pointed out the irony that the senior center will be built there.
"This is a magical moment," Hemstock said, adding that 100 years ago the location was a farm. Then in 1974 the school was built. He said it is interesting to think the first students at the school may benefit in the near-future from what is being built.
2005 was the first mention of a senior housing center in the Town.
Since then, the concept has grown significantly, he stated, plans altering from building a senior center across the street to this location.
Jamie Williams, director of Kent County Economic and Tourism Development traced the history of the property after the school closed in 2017.
The property officially transitioned to the County in May of 2019, she said, then the approximate 24 acres and 36,000 sq ft. building and property were purchased by the Town of Millington in 2022 for $1.
Williams, who told the audience the project speaks to the power of community, collaboration and vision, highlighted the partnerships involved.
The Upper Shore Regional Council provided $50,000 for a preliminary architectural feasibility report.
The Rural Maryland council approved $100,000 for design and engineering cost of the roof and fire suppression system.
The Town of Millington invested $1.4 million for repairs, maintenance, utility cost, staff time, permit fees and submitted a $500,000 community legacy grant application to the DHCD for the construction of the roof and fire suppression system.
Home Partnership Inc. committed over $630,000 towards reconstructing 2200 square ft. for senior-focused spaces.
With all that effort, Williams acknowledged, challenges still remain, estimating the overall cost is projected to be $1.5 million.
She recognized that also includes creating walking trails, a community garden, and creating other enriching open spaces. That takes partnerships, to "build a brighter future for Kent County," she expressed.
After introductions, Secretary Day spoke, expressing the need for this center in an aging population.
"Housing is critical, particularly when we have failed to build housing from 2018 until now," Day said.
Housing costs are high and not likely to decline, he added.
With supply chain interest and expensive labor costs, as all the developers, builders and government officials could attest to, it can be challenging, Day noted.
Day emphasized that with local government all-in, and the developers and community all-in, he knows that Governor Wes Moore would want the DHCD to be all-in, as well.
"We're not at the finish line yet but we are 100% committed," Day reiterated.

title: On The Shore - New Skate Park Could Be Coming To The Shore
author: Will Bontrager
content:
On The Shore - New Skate Park Could Be Coming To The Shore

 September 4, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager | Page: 1 | Section: News

 CHESTERTOWN - Chestertown could soon welcome skateboarders back after previously passing ordinances prohibiting the sport.And a skate park may be in the works.Recently, town officials announced they want to host the skate zone at Gateway Park.This may be to address the issue that within the county, persons 65 years and over make up 28.2 percent of the population."To vitalize the town, we need youth," Chair of the Chestertown Recreation Committee, Jim Bogden said.During an unofficial meeting with Chestertown Recreation Committee members, on Aug. 15, Mark Mumford, retired resident, provided suggestions.He said he's always been amazed at skateboarders, performing tricks in the parking lot.Mumford envisioned Chestertown producing a skatepark similar to Goldsboro Municipal Park. While walking that path, he recorded on his phone some features that impressed him. As committee members Bogden, Frank Rhodes and Danielle Cudone huddled up, he showed them possible ideas to model for their future site."Goldsboro's a town of probably 300 people, but it has a phenomenally laid out park," he said, narrating the video.The park consisted of a flybox, some transitions, (enabling skaters to move from ground position to vertical), a few rails and benches.Mumford pointed out everything in the area's designed to skate on. For example, the benches have metal coping on the edges so skateboarders can grind on them. Even the flower boxes have coping.To get a skatepark in Chestertown, it'll take money, and some politicking, Bogden acknowledged."It's wonderfully isolated," he told the Chestertown council during an earlier meeting in March. "Noise isn't an issue. We'd love for that to become a center for young adults and older teens to be as active and loud as they want to be." He said it would make a great location for a skate park.The County's five-year plan also has room for a skatepark, he noted. They might want to put one in Worton instead, he added. Wherever it's built, he queried, whether it will work this time.Rock Hall and Millington both hosted a skatepark at one time.The first one was built at the Rock Hall Civic Center.It was shut down based on only a few people skating, and had problems with vandalism and litter. They sold their ramps to Millington during their building phase.Millington Skatepark lasted longer, but ultimately, because the park was surrounded by neighbors, not very isolated, and rules could not be maintained, it was demolished in June of 2020.In 2016, that park became a hot button issue. Former Millington Mayor C.J. Morales said, neighbors complained about park users' foul language, suspected drug activity and unsupervised children.According to an article in the Kent County News, now Millington Mayor Kevin Hemstock, who was a Millington councilman at the time, said he was in favor of the skateboard park when it was first built 15 years ago, "but it's been a headache." In addition, Jo Manning, the Millington town administrator said the group responsible for the park did not enforce the rules like registration, payment of fee, and adult supervision requirement. In 2017-19, she said, the council talked about maintenance requirements.The next few years they found the numbers for insurance coverage, repairs/replacement and ongoing maintenance exceeded the cost of the original park.Manning noted although the park was built to keep skateboarders off the streets, they returned.The streets aren't kind to skateboarders in the municipalities.Millington's Town Code, Chapter 50, declares it unlawful for any person to "ride, propel, or push or otherwise operate a skateboard or any similar vehicle on any public way, street, alley, sidewalk, parking lot, or public property." Betterton also had similar issues.According to Betterton Town Administrator Tom Mogle, Betterton's skateboard ordinance was established in 2001, then changed the next year to hold parents accountable for any misdeeds of the youth.Chestertown, however, has never hosted a skate park, and the committee's excited to try.Bogden said for it to happen, the ordinance in Chestertown prohibiting skateboarding needs to be overturned.Chapter 140 in the Chestertown Code of Ordinances reads: "It shall be unlawful for a person to operate, or cause to be operated, roller skates, scooters, skateboards, or sleds on the streets, highways, public parking lots, or other public areas designated for motor vehicle use within the town.Skateboards aren't permitted on the sidewalks either.Despite these ordinances, and some past controversy, the committee is anticipating moving ahead. Plans are to walk Gateway Park with Mumford to get an idea of the space they'd be working with.They're calling for consultants.Committee member Cudone said, "We did our research.What we gather is we need a core of dedicated skateboarders." Bogden and Rhodes were in agreement."The most successful parks are designed from the bottom up, with active, interested users," Bogden said.They urged skateboarders to reach out to them to help with the design process.Chestertown and Millington both are looking at Goldsboro for skatepark ideas.Manning mentioned Millington "decided to create some smaller scale challenges for boarders to use," while they renovate Robvanary Park.They'll be along the walking trail, somewhat similar to the existing park in Goldsboro.Mogle said on a visit to France, he was struck by how skateparks brought families together."I thought it was a brilliant idea to incorporate modes of recreation like rollerblading, scooters, and bikes. This inclusivity expands use and avoids troublesome (mostly false) stereotypes. We need more activities that draw people together, remove stigmas, and allow younger generations to express themselves in ways they find meaningful."

Cacophony or symphony? - Musical instruments for kids at Aunt Sarah's Playground spark noise complaints

 CHESTERTOWN - At Wilmer Park, more precisely, at Aunt Sarah's Playground, there have been complaints by neighbors about excessive noise for the past few months.In the playground there are musical instruments like drums, a xylophone and chimes by PlayEnsemble.Each one is a percussion instrument you strike to create a unique sound. These sounds mixed with disconcerting cries at night, construction rumbles, along with the boat traffic on the Chester river, are reasons some of the neighbors filed an official request to the town for help.Chestertown Manager Larry DiRe summed it up for the mayor and council at the Aug. 7 meeting, "What measures can we take to reduce the sound impact of playing musical instruments and reduce the chance of misuse?" The noise issue at the park was first introduced during a July 3 council meeting. Herz, in charge of Ward 1, had received a letter from neighbors and brought it up for public comment.Some of the neighbors stepped up, speaking candidly about their concerns.Former Chestertown Bank President Ray Tarrach said, "We're trying to have the playground be a better neighbor. People drive up with their lights on. Sometimes at 10:30 p.m. The pavilion is another trouble spot." Tarrach added that activity of a sexual nature occurs at the pavilion often."The whole area needs some attention," he said.Another neighbor, Nancy Bennington, said it's not unusual to hear commotion at night. She had suggested that the town reach out to the manufacturer of the instruments to see what they could do about muffling the sound.She agreed with Tarrach, that lewd activity had increased at the park.Herz clarified to the public, the neighbors' main concern was the noise at night, thus noise created by adults, not children at play during the day. Herz also noted park rules state no soliciting after dusk. He urged those neighbors concerned to call the police when they hear suspicious activity occurring at night."Rules are rules," he said.O'Brien, the liaison for the Chestertown Recreation Committee, said the nature of the instruments themselves is part of the problem.The mayor said this was the first playground they had adjacent to houses. "We should have checked with the neighbors about the sound," he acknowledged.Herz met with the Recreation Committee formally on July 18. By this meeting, comments had escalated on social media over the topic.Herz told the commission, "In the whirlwind of social media, this issue has been whipped around that we, (the council and the neighbors), want the musical instruments removed. But having spoken to many of these residents, I think what they're asking for is just a little understanding." And many of those concerned residents like Frankie Mayo, brought forward constructive solutions. Mayo suggested using a sound-absorbing material, Dynamat, used by custom car companies and found in the walls of musical rooms in schools to muffle the sound.Other similar ideas were brought up."I want to say what a rich discussion this has been. I really appreciate all the people coming out to contribute," Commission President Chair Jim Bogden said, encouraged by the participation and constructive solutions.DiRe reported during the Aug. 7 meeting with council, across social media platforms, the results were over 1,000 comments, the majority of them supporting keeping the playground equipment.He said the committee wanted to work collaboratively with the community and went into further detail about the Dynamat material."It's relatively low cost at $200," he added.One of the playground instruments, an electric guitar, DiRe noted they're looking for ways to reduce the amplification; f no solution is found, however, he said they will talk about its removal.There are other ways to muffle the sound than altering the instruments, he noted, suggesting landscaping around the playground area as one way to soften the noise.And the town manager told the council, it is indeed noisy there. He said on his visit on Aug. 3, around 11:45 p.m., there was constant noise from power boats on the river and ongoing construction.However, the noise is not the only problem at Wilmer Park, as earlier, the neighbors and the council members commented about the sexual activity in the pavilion and parking lot.To prevent nighttime loiterers, DiRe said physical barriers, such as a swinging gate with a timer at dusk and dawn, might be effective.The cost, he said, would be between $600 and $2,000, which doesn't include installation cost or the expertise of an electrician.From the review of the town council meetings, the recreation committee, and the comments from the town manager, it appears that nobody wishes to remove the instruments, and stop children from having a good time.They just want to come to a peaceful conclusion for everybody in the town.Foster said, "There's always going to be noise there. Boats, construction, but we've got to get it back to near-normal."

title: Betterton Pushes Back: Town Says Halo Solar Plan Would Threaten Safety, Growth and Historic Character
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Betterton pushes back: Town says Halo Solar plan would threaten safety, growth and historic character

 October 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 1060
 Words 

 Read News Document

 BETTERTON — Residents of this small Kent County town say they support renewable energy — just not in the middle of their gateway.On Sept. 9, nearly two dozen people joined an online public hearing before the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC) to oppose a proposal from Halo Solar LLC. The company is seeking a certificate of public convenience and necessity (CPCN) to construct a 5-megawatt solar generating facility at the corner of Howell Point and Still Pond-Betterton roads — an area town officials say is the last viable space for residential and commercial growth.
Presiding over the hearing was Public Utility Law Judge Christine Burke, who first heard from Halo representatives before opening the floor to community comments.
Town officials: "Not at this location"
Betterton leaders emphasized they are not opposed to solar power but strongly object to this site, which they called the "gateway to Betterton." The town, population 298, has been working for years to balance conservation with limited development.
"This town has been incorporated for almost 120 years, going from a popular tourist attraction to residential," said Councilman Wayne Gilchrest. "This project would be sealing the town's fate for at least ten years."
Mayor Donald Sutton said the proposed structure would block the town's designated helicopter landing zone, posing a public safety risk. "It's zoned residential and commercial — the only area we have for expansion," Sutton said. He proposed a compromise: scale the solar farm down to 10 acres, leaving 20 available for future development.
Town Manager Tom Mogle added that Betterton's award-winning wastewater treatment plant, built in 2017, depends on new dwellings to offset its high operating costs. "We've invested heavily — rebuilding the boardwalk, restoring the bathhouse, improving Ericsson Avenue — all with a vision of balancing conservation with growth," he said.
Developer presents plan
Michael Lossia, a founder of Halo Solar, gave a brief presentation describing "Betterton Solar" as a 15-foot-high array of bifacial panels on a single-axis tracking system surrounded by fencing, evergreens, and other vegetation. The project, engineered by Kimley-Horn, is one of 15 Halo developments on Maryland's Eastern Shore.
"With that, I'll turn it back to you, Judge," Lossia said after a short summary — leaving residents eager to respond.
Residents: "A bad idea for a small town"
Helen Martin, who lives about 125 feet from the proposed site, said the project would destroy local ecosystems, cause soil erosion, and disrupt migratory bird patterns. "It's only six blocks from the beach — our biggest tourist attraction," she said. "Betterton is on the National Register of Historic Places. We need to keep that charm."
John Erikson questioned why a commercial solar farm would be allowed in a residential community. "There's a reason these projects aren't built in towns," he said. "This would be the only one like it in Kent County."
Paul Falcon, who lives directly across from the parcel, presented photos showing what he described as an "unsightly" buffer of fencing and metal panels. "The facility would be the size of five Walmart Supercenters," he said. "It would dominate the landscape, taking up one-third of the town's footprint. Are we expected to live with something that looks like a strip mine?"
Concerns over planning, housing, and costs
Professional planner Creigh Rahekamp argued the project would undermine the county's need for workforce housing. "Employers already struggle to find skilled workers because housing is too expensive," he said. "Halo picked the one site in town that eliminates its only growth opportunity. That's completely wrong."
Retired teacher David Paltrineri compared the situation to Middletown, Delaware, where an Amazon warehouse spurred traffic and overcrowding. "I saw firsthand what happens when growth is driven by outside interests without careful planning," he said.
Resident Kathryn Klvana said she was shocked to learn the state could override local zoning. She also questioned the validity of Halo's impact studies, saying glare analyses failed to consider larger vehicles such as trucks, farm equipment, or crop-dusting planes. She warned that stormwater runoff could carry contaminants into a Department of Natural Resources critical area and questioned what would happen in the event of a fire.
Klvana and others also feared higher energy costs and lower property values.
Loss of landing zone sparks safety fears
Art Pleasanton, representing the Betterton Volunteer Fire Company, said the proposed solar site would eliminate the town's emergency helicopter landing zone — a crucial asset during summer rescues.
"The biggest day this summer, we had 1,000 people on the beach," he said. "When a young girl nearly drowned, lifeguards pulled her out, gave CPR, and we airlifted her from that field. Her life was saved. If we lose that zone, the next one is 7.3 miles away — a 14-minute trip. Save our landing zone so we can save lives."
Property values and land use
Several speakers cited studies showing homes near large solar fields lose an average of 8% of their property value. Retired engineer Douglas Cregar said Halo had purchased enough land to host a 7-megawatt system, far larger than proposed.
Janet Christensen-Lewis, chair of the Kent Conservation and Preservation Alliance, said the project would "hamstring a well-governed town's growth agenda in favor of an extractive corporate use."
She noted that Maryland's Chapter 623 directs regulators to weigh renewable energy benefits against the loss of scarce housing land. "Halo will get guaranteed income from subscribers," she said. "Betterton residents get first dibs on subscriptions — crumbs."
A call for the PSC to visit
Pat Whitmore urged the commission to look beyond Betterton. "This isn't happening in isolation," she said. "Halo has projects in Kennedyville, Rock Hall, and Warwick. They're taking farmland and siting projects on town growth areas. Why not build on developed land like landfills?"
Tom Deliberto, a Betterton Planning Commission member and attorney, called the project's energy contribution negligible. "The gain to Maryland's renewable portfolio is 11-thousandths of 1 percent," he said. "Proportionally, it's like taking 34 square miles of Baltimore County for a fraction of a percent of power."
Mark Mendez of Glen Street made the final appeal: "This is your chance to say no. Come see the town — see how out of place this would be."
Next steps
Judge Burke closed the session by reminding participants that all comments — oral, mailed, or electronic — will be considered when she drafts her proposal order. Additional comments can be submitted through Dec. 8, following an in-person hearing scheduled for Dec. 1 (location to be determined).
Case documents and comment forms are available on the PSC website at psc.state.md.us, under Case No. 9786.

title: Kent Commissioners Oppose Striped Bass Limits
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Kent commissioners oppose striped bass limits

 September 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 570
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — On Aug. 29, the Kent County commissioners signed a letter expressing their opposition to proposed striped bass (rockfish) limits, sending it to Maryland Natural Resources Secretary Josh Kurtz.The commissioners voiced opposition to the Fishery Management Plan amendment that proposes a 12% reduction in the harvest of striped bass.
They said the changes would reduce the commercial fishing industry's ability to harvest striped bass by 58%.
The letter objected to new regulations allowing catch-and-release fishing from January through May, a period that has been closed the past six years to protect spawning fish. The commissioners said the policy contradicts the Maryland Department of Natural Resources' proposal last year to safeguard spawning stock biomass with a 2029 recovery goal.
They added that Kent County's recreational and charter boat industry would be hurt by a non-targeting closure from July 15 to Aug. 31, when boats would be prohibited from catching rockfish. That closure normally lasts two weeks.
"This is unnecessary and will create significant hardships for the industry, economic tourism in the county and income generated by fishers," the letter stated.
ECONOMIC IMPACTCommission President Ron Fithian, a longtime waterman, said they have already heard of cancellations and reductions in reserved trips for charter boats.
"The economic impact on our county and its waterfront businesses will bear financial losses," Fithian said. "It will erode the economic growth we have worked so hard to develop."
Although the fisheries have faced regulatory reductions in the past, commissioners called the latest proposals a "tipping point," predicting some food businesses may close for good.
Commissioner John Price said, "Unfortunately the Department of Natural Resources is not going to be satisfied until they run the commercial watermen and charter boats out of business."
Price compared the situation to waterfowl hunting, where DNR has allowed Sunday hunting instead of providing a rest and nesting period for birds.
Fithian said he has fought similar issues his entire life, calling it "death by a thousand cuts." He said DNR enacts new regulations year after year without evidence to support them.
The letter concluded with a call for state officials to support Kent County's small business community: "Kent County is open for business, and we want to keep it that way."
INDUSTRY RESPONSERob Newberry, chair of the Delmarva Fisheries Association, said the proposed amendment makes changes to Maryland's recreational season baseline that are harmful to both commercial and charter operations.
He accused the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, DNR and the Coastal Conservation Association Maryland of hypocrisy, saying their policies disturb spawning rockfish while claiming to conserve them.
"If they allow rockfish to be disturbed during the spawning season, they are not conserving anything," Newberry said. "It's counterproductive."
He criticized the Coastal Conservation Association, saying its actions prioritize finances and recreation over fish health and the industry's future.
Newberry said if the amendment is passed the industry will face "severe limitations."
"It's a complete disaster," he said. "And it is inexplicable."
PUBLIC HEARINGS
Newberry emphasized that no final decision has been made. A public hearing is scheduled for Sept. 23 at the Michael E. Busch Library in Annapolis, which has a seating capacity of 200.
"We are trying to get as many to attend as possible to tell DNR we do not support this amendment," Newberry said.
The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission will meet Oct. 23-24 to make its final decision.
Maryland Department of Natural Resources Associate Director Michael Luisi said since the commissioners' letter was addressed to Kurtz, a response will come following review by the agency's Office of Communications.

content:
As solar looms on horizon, Betterton residents weigh in ahead of public hearing

 September 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 BETTERTON — For the past two Saturday afternoons, residents living near Betterton held informal meetings discussing Halo Betterton Solar LLC.Halo Betterton LLC had submitted an application in April for a 5-megawatt solar project on a 30-acre site at Howell Point Road and Still Pond-Betterton Road which, if built, will be directly across from some of these neighbors.
As brought up in previous council meetings, the town is opposed to the project because the company's plans do not fit with Betterton's comprehensive plan. It takes away any potential to have commercial development in that area.
The informal meetings were conducted by Paul Falcon and Kathryn Klvana at 13959 Still Pond Road and then at the Betterton Volunteer Firehouse, and drew out other neighbors who would be affected by building the installation.
The second meeting that took place at the firehouse was well-attended and included Mayor Donald Sutton, council member Gerry Werner, longtime residents and people passionate about this cause coming from other Maryland regions affected by these facilities.
Sutton said it is good to see so many people come out and express their concerns.
Residents raised multiple objections to the proposed solar installation during the meetings.

"We've done our research and are against this solar installation here," Cregar said. "Studies show that everyone within a mile will lose 5% in property value. Art Pleasanton raised concerns about emergency services, noting the proposed site would interfere with helicopter medical evacuations.
"If (solar) is built where they want to build it they'd have to do it over a helicopter landing zone," Pleasanton said. "The next nearest one is at Worton at the school. For anyone who thinks this is not an issue, last year a little girl was saved from drowning because we had a way to get her out fast."
Kathryn Klvana expressed frustration with recent state legislation that could override local zoning decisions.
"I'm shocked that with this new law Governor Wes Moore just signed, the state can override local zoning and put this huge solar farm across from our homes," Klvana said. "We moved to this beautiful place to retire. We're zoned community residential. What about our rights?"

Residents challenge solar project over zoning, health risks

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News

 The Maryland Public Service Commission heard residents' concerns Tuesday over a proposed community solar project on 41 acres of a 199-acre property at 10066 Peacock Corner Road in Millington, owned by David Chance.The project, designated TPE MD KE51, is being developed by Turning Point Energy (TPE), a renewable energy firm that has spearheaded several solar initiatives in Maryland, including a second proposal in Kennedyville. According to company information, Turning Point focuses on sustainable, ground-mounted solar projects designed to expand clean energy access in the region.
More than a dozen residents gathered at Galena Elementary School at 7 p.m. for the PSC hearing, moderated by Chief Public Utility Law Judge Chuck McLean. In addition to Turning Point representatives, legal counsel, and project managers, officials from the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, Kent County Attorney Tom Yeager and Planning, Housing and Zoning deputy Carla Gerber were in attendance.
After brief introductions by Turning Point's team, Yeager and Gerber outlined the county's position. Yeager noted that local zoning restricts solar projects in this agriculture district to five acres and contended that Turning Point should have applied for a special exception. Project manager Frances Yuhas said the company was aware of the five‐acre limit for utility-scale solar in the district and chose not to seek an exception, adding that final approval lies with the Public Service Commission under state preemption.
Resident Darryl Calloway expressed his concern, saying, "I would love someone to address the health concerns I have such as microwaves. Anyone who lives near these arrays, what happens to them?"
Certified solar thermal engineer Dick Durham raised additional issues about panel efficiency and recycling challenges, noting that the panels contain materials such as lead and cadmium telluride. He also warned that pending legislation, Senate Bill 0931, could reshape land-use controls in ways reminiscent of eminent domain.
When asked about the origin of the panels, Yuhas said production could occur in the United States but noted that international manufacturing — including in Mexico or China —remains a possibility. Maryland Department of Natural Resources official Ginny Rogers addressed environmental risk concerns, stating, "From what we see there is no risk at all involved," and outlined plans to plant native, pollinator-friendly ground cover to boost biodiversity.
Kennedyville resident Judi Gifford questioned the economic benefits of the array, asking, "Are there any savings for residents at all?" Yuhas replied that subscribers to the power would be guaranteed a 5 to 10 percent discount over a 25-year subscription. Gerber added that the county would likely reclassify the property as commercial rather than agricultural, potentially increasing tax revenue.
At the hearing, Turning Point announced they committed to a $52,000 donation to Kent County's agricultural preservation program — a request based on state law calculations of agricultural value. Representatives from the company stayed afterward to discuss next steps pending a PSC decision on their certificate of public convenience and necessity.
When asked how they felt the county received their project proposal, TPE representative, Attorney Margaret Witherup of Witherup Allen Law admitted, "It's hard to tell. Each site is different."
No other comment were received from Turning Point legal counsel, Attorney Witherup, or from representatives at Kimley-Horn and Associates, Inc. Kent County officials said they will continue to monitor developments in the project. More details can be found under Case No. 9742 at the Maryland PSC website.

"We're not opposed to alternative forms of energy, just not in Betterton," said council member Gerry Werner. "Especially not in the only area that could be zoned residential and commercial for our future expansion."

In nearby Chestertown, officials faced similar challenges when the Public Service Commission approved a 245-acre solar system on Morgnec Road, despite opposition from both town and county governments.
"If there is well-expressed public sentiment against building this here, maybe the power company will cut their losses," Werner said. He is researching what rights, if any, the town has in the matter.
Meanwhile, Millington is further along in its solar facility process. A second public hearing is scheduled for Feb. 17 regarding the KE51 project, which would occupy part of a 199-acre property. That project, designated as a Community Solar Energy Generating System, would deliver power to subscribers via the Delmarva Power electric distribution grid.
The Public Service Commission maintains final authority over solar facility approvals, though it must consider local jurisdiction input in its decisions.

 CHESTERTOWN — On July 11, there will be a public hearing at the Kent County Courthouse for an issue that has been lying dormant for two years — the construction of a solar panel farm on Morgnec Road.Urban Grid is located in the central portion of Kent County, east of Chestertown. If all goes to the company's plan, Morgnec Solar LLC, owned by Urban Grid, will connect to the power grid via an existing Delmarva Power Substation adjacent to the project site.
The state recently approved of the project against the county and Chestertown's wishes.
Urban Grid's website lists the benefits of a solar field.
"The project will yield significant Real Property Tax revenue for Kent County for a lifetime," it says, along with listing the environmental benefits of solar power.
The project poses "no material impact to the wetlands, cultural resources or threatens any endangered species," according to Urban Grid.
Architect Tom Kocubinski and chair of the Kent County Conservation and Preservation Alliance Janet Christensen-Lewis would beg to differ.
"It's 140,000 solar collectors. That's a mile long," Kocubinski said.
Not only do they disapprove now, he added, but the Kent County Commissioners did when the issue came up roughly two years ago.
On Feb. 1, 2022, at their regular meeting, the commissioners joined Kent Conservation and Preservation Alliance in an appeal of the Public Service Commission's approval of a certificate of public convenience and necessity for the Morgnec Road Solar project.
And Chestertown was not on board either. Mayor David Foster didn't see it as a suitable location at the time since eastward is their only direction to expand.
Foster said, "While we normally welcome solar power, the town also opposed that solar project because it was right in the middle of our only real opportunity for expansion of Chestertown."
Kocubinski and others thought the issue was settled. However, a year ago a judge approved of the project, leading to heated discussions over the solar farm.
Those for the project say that these solar panels will save money and allow the community to "think globally while living locally." They say that it will boost the economy, bringing revenue to a county desperate for it.
Opponents claim solar panel energy is not as environmentally friendly as once thought.
The solar panels utilize numerous materials — cobalt, nickel, cadmium, lithium, vanadium, graphite — the mining of which has been shown to damage the environment.
Opponents also point out once in operation, the solar field will be controlled from a distance, not by people in the county.
Instead of a solar farm of one mile frontage on Morgnec Road with a screening wall, KCPA proposes an alternative of berm, trees, shrubs and pedestrian amenities like a footpath.
All of this is likely to be discussed on July 11 at 1:30 p.m.

title: Caroline Commissioners Discuss Landfill, Solar Batteries
author: Tom McCall
content:
Caroline commissioners discuss landfill, solar batteries

 May 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Life 
 
 568

 DENTON — At their May 7 meeting, the Caroline County Commissioners extended a moratorium on solar array batteries and finalized an agreement to retain the regional landfill for another 18 years.Caroline County has agreed to 2042 being the end of life for its landfill. Mid-shore II Regional Landfill is governed by a four-county agreement between Queen Anne's, Kent, Talbot and Caroline counties.
In the late 1980s, due to new federal regulations, the counties had to close their landfills and replace them with new landfills. In response to this new regulation, Talbot, Caroline and Queen Anne's counties engaged with MES to form a partnership where each county would take turns hosting a landfill for a 20-year term. Kent County later joined that partnership.
Caroline County is hosting the current landfill and, under the original arrangement, would be off the hook at the end of 2030 when Queen Anne's County would take over the responsibility of host. However, the partnering counties have agreed to allow the landfill to stay in Caroline County for 12 years longer than initially planned.
Dan Fox, deputy administrator, said the county will receive a revenue increase of around $12.3 million over the duration of the extended agreement. The counties agreed on a $3 per ton post fee until 2030. In 2031 it will rise to $6.
"That is a big number as far as our budget," Fox said.
Commissioner Larry Porter said the increased revenue will be helpful as he looks to the future of Caroline County's finances.
"The tipping point is knowing what is coming down the road to the county from a financial standpoint. The Blueprint numbers for education, the numbers for the budget projections that will start this fiscal year from the state," Porter said. "It has been our goal to have maintained property tax rates. We have done this for eight years and are going to do it again this year. Beyond that we cannot control the additional things that will be mandated by the state of Maryland. To turn away the opportunity to generate revenue without raising property tax rate is something we have to consider."
The next action agenda item was solar energy batteries and the commissioners' belief that they are dangerous.
The commissioners extended a moratorium on the batteries until March 31, 2025. Explaining this decision, they said that the local fire departments and first responders are not equipped and staffed to safely deal with these energy storage systems were they to catch on fire.
"When the electric is generated from the solar panels, if it is not distributed to the grid, it is stored in batteries that are then stored in, like, large storage containers," Porter said. "How would it be addressed if those storage facilities were malfunctioning and caught on fire?"
He said the moratorium will remain in place until these batteries can safely be put in place.
During public comments, James Baker brought up the issue of what to do with a solar energy battery at the end of its 20 year life cycle. He said he thought it would cost taxpayers.
At the May 7 meeting, the commissioners also made two proclamations. The first was to Ken Eaton and Mark Kerzener, who represented the Mid-Shore chapter of A Brotherhood Against Totalitarian Enactments of Maryland. The commissioners proclaimed May a month for motorcycle safety and awareness.
The other proclamation went to Derek Simmons, superintendent of Caroline County Public Schools. It was a proclamation for teacher appreciation month.

title: Caroline Commissioners Hear Options for Landfill After 2030
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Caroline commissioners hear options for landfill after 2030

 April 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 785
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County could remain the host of the regional landfill for 12 years longer than originally planned.At a Caroline County Commissioners meeting Tuesday morning, Queen Anne's County Administrator Todd Mohn, CPA and Queen Anne's County Consultant Joe Zimmerman and Queen Anne's County Commissioner James Moran came to speak about the possibility of using the Mid-Shore II Regional Landfill in Ridgely through 2042 rather than building a new landfill in Queen Anne's County for 2031.
During their presentation, Mohn said Maryland Environmental Service has been working with county administrators to evaluate the future of Mid-Shore II, and it has concluded that the landfill could "easily provide service" to the citizens of the region through approximately 2042.
The Mid-Shore II landfill, which was opened in 2011, provides services to Talbot, Caroline, Queen Anne's and Kent counties.
Mohn explained that in the late 1980s, due to new federal regulations, the counties had to close their landfills and and replace them with new landfills. In response to this new regulation, Talbot, Caroline and Queen Anne's counties engaged with MES to form a partnership where each county would take turns hosting a landfill for a 20-year term. Kent County later joined that partnership.
Caroline County is hosting the current landfill and, under the original arrangement, would be off the hook at the end of 2030 when Queen Anne's County would take over the responsibility of host. However, if the partnering counties agreed, they could instead extend the lifetime of Caroline County's landfill.
During the presentation, Mohn listed reasons why Queen Anne's County feels this option makes sense. For Caroline County, he said that this option would provide economic stability for Ridgely businesses and that the county would get a host fee for the extension of service.
He said the option would also maximize the value of public infrastructure, defer liability for debt to construct a new landfill, maintain shorter haul routes for Talbot County and avoid the cost of a transfer operation.
Moran said landfills are at a premium.
"We want to maximize that," he said about the space in each landfill. "And if this (provides) us with an extra 30 years of life that we didn't have coming into this 80-year deal, then that's a good thing for the environment, it's a good thing for the Eastern Shore."
If this proposal moves forward, all of the partnering counties would need to come to an agreement on a modified arrangement, including the host fee for Caroline County.
At the meeting, Zimmerman presented three options for host fees and annual tipping fee increases for the Mid-Shore II landfill:
A host fee of $2 per ton of waste growing to $4 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.15% in tipping fees.A host fee of $3 per ton of waste growing to $5 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.35% in tipping fees.A host fee of $4 per ton of waste growing to $6 after 2031 with an annual increase of 1.5% in tipping fees.
"We think these are achievable options," Zimmerman said about the three options. "It's really the question of how much risk the counties want to take on in terms of their competitive posture."
He said that historically, tipping fees have, on average, annually increased by 1.42%.
Caroline County Commission President Travis Breeding said he has made it clear to MES that he agrees with keeping the landfill operating in Caroline County for environmental and economic reasons, but he would like to make sure the county retains "any of the savings associated with the extension of the landfill."
He said the county's residents are the ones burdened with the affects of the landfill operations, including truck traffic and bad smells from time to time.
Commission Vice President Larry Porter spoke about the impact of MES operations on the county.
He said that although this proposal is an opportunity to generate more revenue without raising property taxes, having the landfill in the county has affected the condition of the roads where trash is being driven, including trash left on those roads. He said the extension of the landfill's services would be a hard sell to the public.
"For me, anything that we do is going to have to involve MES stepping up to the plate and fulfilling what I think the obligations and responsibilities are," he said, adding that roads would be part of that obligation, in his mind.
Porter asked the presenters if it appears that the other partnering counties are on board with keeping the landfill in Caroline County and paying a host fee. Mohn said everyone seems to be in agreement.
"The question is, what is that host fee going to be?" Mohn said.
Porter said the county will have a public hearing on this in the future. He did not give a date.

title: 'Team effort' is what it takes to build and retain businesses in Kent
author: WILL BONTRAGER
content:
'Team effort' is what it takes to build and retain businesses in Kent

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 912

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — In a recent interview, Jamie Williams noted that in Kent County, businesses are coming and going regularly."It's a churning process," she acknowledged.
For instance, Rock City Cafe's last day was Oct 12. Then Oct. 15, at that same location, 21536 Rock Hall Ave., Little Lemon Leaf Diner is advertising a hiring event, for kitchen and dining room.
Some new businesses moved in recently as well. Starbucks is now open for business, and It's Masala Time, an Indian restaurant at 3 Washington Square, had its soft opening on Wednesday, Oct. 2.
As director of Kent County Department of Economic and Tourism Development for 11 years, Williams sees this turnaround daily, offering support and creating opportunities for businesses to thrive.
While working with the Economic Commission, business owners and leaders in the community appointed by the county commissioners provide guidance and insight.
Their goals line up with the county's comprehensive plan: to retain and expand businesses while supporting start-up businesses.
With a hefty schedule to close out the week, Williams, highlighted some projects her staff is working on.
Millington Senior Housing: The Millington Senior Village is a project that will provide 52 one-story apartments for people age 62 and up.
The project is located on land once part of the Millington Elementary School property.
The county is working with Millington during the grant search process. If successful, they hope to build a community resource center, food pantry, church and daycare center, centralizing services in one location.
With all that activity, Williams hopes to have Delmarva Community Transit services to accommodate residential needs.
"The more density we have the more services we can build there," Williams commented.
Railroad Upgrade: Williams pointed out the Worton railroad system, services five companies and was in a state of disrepair for quite a while. The county had received funding from the state to fix the tracks in May of 2020.
Williams was happy to announce that in September 2024 that project is finally completed.
The fact that from the time they had received the funding to the actual repair was four years, she said, should give an indication to the public of how slow-going these processes sometimes take.
Brownfield Properties: Williams and staff has identified 12 brownfield properties — places contaminated and needing remediation.
Most of these properties, the director said, were dry-cleaning establishments, dealing with chemicals. One of these is in Chestertown, Admiral Cleaners, located across from the 7-Eleven on 212 Maple Ave.; a building that sits dormant with graffiti on the walls.
Williams asked, is it worth the county adopting a brownfield credit, a state program. Is it worth going through that kind of process to redevelop the properties?
They are seeking answers to those pressing questions.
Recreational Cannabis: Beginning July 1, 2023, individuals in Maryland at least age 21 could legally use and possess the personal use amount of cannabis. Licensing is issued by the State for those who aim to start a dispensary.
Currently, Williams said the county issued only one micro-license, for a cannabis dispensary in Millington.
According to earlier reports, the establishment is under Rahul "Rocky" Dutta and if meeting all the requirements, will be located in the vacant Truist Bank building at 400 Cypress Street.
In talking with Dutta earlier in the week, Williams reported everything is moving forward.
Short-term rental tax:The county has been working with the municipalities to collect short-term rental tax from properties where AirBnb's or Vrbo properties or other rentals of that nature are located.
Williams acknowledged that is an extensive process involving lots of moving parts.
She had worked with her administrative specialist Rose Osborn to locate the properties throughout the county. They purchased software to track these properties more efficiently as well as send out notices.
Now it seems like they are seeing positive results.
According to the July report, Williams said "64 percent of properties are in compliance."
The director expects higher in the future.
"We feel we're going to see the biggest impact after the September numbers."
Other than using the tracking software, they worked closely with the municipalities to coordinate their memorandum of understandings for short-term rental tax, so they are all on the same page.
The county collects the taxes monthly and remit it to the towns. The towns receive 90 percent of the revenue with 10 percent going to the county for administrative costs.
Even before they purchased the software, Williams and Osborn have been working steadily on this issue since November 2022.
She was thankful for the cooperation that occurred since then.
"Getting all five towns together is an example of what we need to be doing for a lot of other projects," she said.
Business Retention and Expansion: Williams maintained they have always responded to the needs of business owners. However, now, that attention and focus is being formalized as they launch their Business and Retention Visit Program, starting last week.
The department has reached out to 10 or 11 businesses so far, refining their data-gathering process and consulting with business owners.
They've been all over the county, visiting KRM Development, Hickory Stick and Blue Heron Oyster House to name a few.
The qualitative information they gather will be assessed and used to help the community.
All of this would not be possible without Economic Development Manager Katie Abbott, the Kent County Chamber of Commerce and many others, Williams noted.
"It takes a collaborative effort from everyone; that's how economic development happens."
As a team, they are helping businesses find their niche area to succeed in a region specific to rural concerns.
"We're not an area to put up a big distribution center," Williams said."We're here to promote businesses focusing on what's unique and special in Kent County."

title: Everbridge Becomes Kent's New Emergency Alert System
author: Will Bontrager
content:
Everbridge becomes Kent's new emergency alert system

 September 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 607

 CHESTERTOWN — Even at 3 a.m. from his home, with a tap of a button Emergency Preparedness Planner Brian Pearsall can send out an alert to a majority of Kent County residents.He hopes he never has to do that, but it's beneficial the option's there.
In the basement of the Kent County Sheriff's Office, where the Office of Emergency Services is housed, he demonstrates how efficient he can be in sending notifications with the department's new software, Everbridge.
On July 1, they made the switch from their old system Code Red, a commendable program in its own right.
Why the switch?
"It allows us to be more effective to the community with updated information regarding weather forecasts and gives us a larger environment to do that with their technology," Pearsall said.
Pearsall explained there are three levels of communication.
Everbridge is a TSP level 3 certification, designated Public Health, and receives restoration priority just under Federal government certifications. It is required to be backed up and restored in order to provide for public health.
He pointed out, Everbridge is used widely throughout the state right now making communicating between counties convenient.
"We can coordinate better as far as resource needs," Pearsall said.
Everbridge can target specific areas within the county as well.
In a simulation, a test, on his cell phone, Pearsall uses the map on the Everbridge application to send out a storm warning to just Kennedyville residents.
Narrowing it down even further, if needed, he could send notifications to just a specific housing community within Kennedyville.
These alerts are available to residents who have phones in a contract with Everbridge. But also residents can receive specific notifications by signing up to receive alerts at https://www.kentcounty.com/oes.
Those who sign up get alerts for weather conditions, tornados, flash floods, and even water line repairs and other infrastructure information.
So far, the new software has gone off without a hitch as they've sent out 10 alerts since the time of the interview in late August.
Along with other administrators, Director Pete Landon and Chief of Communications Brad Russum, Pearsall meets regularly over Zoom with the Everbridge team to increase their knowledge of technology which always seems to be adapting.
The emergency team is always looking to learn as much as they can to increase the public's awareness and safety.
Like for example, in a few months time they will be able to provide IPAUS, Integrated Public Alert and Warning System.
"When you receive an amber alert on your phone, you can't stop that from coming through. So soon I'll be able to provide this to our residents and visitors," Pearsall remarked.
In the case of an impending tornado for example, he can interrupt every phone in Kent County warning residents.
He's been taking FEMA courses online, and when the time comes, will take an exam for certification along with quarterly tests.
The team's also looking to expand public's awareness like the recent Maryland Mesonet Weather Station, set up at the back of the A.F. Whitsitt Center. It's one of 70 weather stations in the state in partnership with the University of Maryland, Maryland Department of Emergency Management, Maryland Environmental Service and Maryland Department of Health.
These stations are spaced about 10 miles apart and solar powered, measuring rainfall, snow, even the temperature of the top soil.
"It has all manner of capabilities and allows us to be more effective in predicting and forecasting weather events," Pearsall added.
Like the Everbridge program, the station provides opportunities to cooperate with various local, state and federal entities.
All these expansions are part of an effort, "To create a safer Kent County by getting the resources to the community, residents and visitors."
Pearsall noted, "We're doing everything we can to ensure the public is safe as possible."
